options.explanation: Advanced parameters are charged and add policies and larger values that this workload does not need; standard tier is free.

options.text: Store the values in per-environment JSON objects in Amazon S3 encrypted with SSE-KMS and read them at startup
options.explanation: SSE-KMS encrypts whole objects, so per-value access control and encryption only for the sensitive 20 values are lost.

explanation: Parameter Store standard-tier parameters carry no additional charge, support hierarchies such as /prod/app/ for organization and IAM scoping, and SecureString encrypts the sensitive values with AWS KMS; ECS and Lambda can read them directly. Secrets Manager charges per secret for rotation features nobody needs, the advanced tier is billed, and S3 objects lose per-value control. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html

prompt:
A company has 60 accounts in AWS Organizations and adds new accounts every week. The security team must make sure that every internet-facing Application Load Balancer and CloudFront distribution, including those in accounts created later, is protected by the team's baseline AWS WAF rules. Application teams may add their own rules but must be unable to remove the baseline.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the baseline web ACL to each account with CloudFormation StackSets and ask application teams to associate it
options.explanation: StackSets can create the web ACL, but it relies on teams to associate it and does nothing to stop them removing it later.

options.text: Deploy an AWS Config rule that flags load balancers and distributions without the web ACL and remediates them
options.explanation: AWS Config detects and repairs after the fact, so resources run unprotected until a remediation completes.

options.text: Create an AWS Firewall Manager AWS WAF policy with the baseline as its first rule groups, scoped to the organization
Attach a service control policy that denies wafv2:DisassociateWebACL to each OU in the organization
options.explanation: The SCP blocks removal of an association but never creates one, so new resources and accounts start unprotected.

explanation: Firewall Manager, run from a Firewall Manager administrator account, applies an AWS WAF policy to every in-scope resource across the organization and keeps applying it as accounts and resources are added; the policy's first and last rule groups are managed centrally, while account owners can add rules in between. StackSets and SCPs do not attach the rules to new resources, and AWS Config only repairs after a gap. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/fms-chapter.html

prompt:
A software provider runs a TCP-based API in its own VPC and must offer it to about 150 customers, each in their own AWS account and VPC. Many customer VPCs use the same CIDR range as each other and as the provider's VPC. Customers must reach only this one API, the provider must be unable to open connections into customer VPCs, and the traffic must stay off the internet.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Front the API with a Network Load Balancer, publish it as a VPC endpoint service, and have customers create interface endpoints
Create a VPC peering connection from the provider VPC to each customer VPC and allow the API port in the security groups
options.explanation: VPC peering is impossible between VPCs whose CIDR blocks overlap, and a peering route exposes more than the one API.

options.text: Attach every customer VPC and the provider VPC to a transit gateway and use separate route tables for each customer
options.explanation: Transit gateway routing cannot tell identical customer CIDRs apart for return traffic, and it gives network-level reach beyond one API.

options.text: Share the API's subnets with each customer account through AWS Resource Access Manager and let customers launch into them
options.explanation: VPC subnet sharing works only within one organization, and it places customers inside the provider's VPC rather than their own.

explanation: With AWS PrivateLink the provider fronts the API with a Network Load Balancer and publishes an endpoint service; each customer creates an interface endpoint that gets private IPs from its own subnets, so overlapping CIDRs do not matter, only the API is exposed, and connections can be opened only from the consumer side. Peering fails on overlapping CIDRs, a transit gateway cannot route identical ranges apart, and subnet sharing is limited to one organization. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/privatelink-share-your-services.html

prompt:
Workloads in private subnets reach the internet through a NAT gateway in a public subnet. A new policy allows outbound HTTPS only to a short list of partner domains whose IP addresses change often. The control must still hold if a compromised workload uses its own DNS server instead of the Route 53 Resolver.

Which TWO steps together meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the NAT gateway that allows requests whose Host header matches the partner domains
options.explanation: AWS WAF protects resources such as load balancers and CloudFront; it cannot be associated with a NAT gateway.

options.text: Create a Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule group that allows the partner domains and blocks any other domain
options.explanation: DNS Firewall filters queries sent to the Route 53 Resolver; a workload using its own DNS server or a known IP bypasses it.

options.text: Deploy AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain list rule group that allows the partner domains by TLS SNI
Send the NAT gateway subnet's internet route through the firewall endpoint and route return traffic back through it
Restrict outbound HTTPS in the security groups to a managed prefix list holding the partners' current IPs
options.explanation: Security groups match IP addresses, not domains, so a prefix list of partner IPs goes stale as those addresses change.

explanation: AWS Network Firewall's stateful domain list rule group reads the TLS SNI (and HTTP Host) of each connection, so an allow list of domains is enforced on the traffic itself regardless of which DNS server the workload used; it only sees traffic that the route tables send through its firewall endpoints, both outbound and on the return path from the internet gateway. DNS Firewall can be bypassed with another resolver, WAF cannot attach to a NAT gateway, and IP-based security group rules go stale. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/network-firewall/latest/developerguide/stateful-rule-groups-domain-names.html

prompt:
A company must inspect all inbound internet traffic to an application VPC with a third-party firewall appliance that its auditors have approved, running on Amazon EC2. The appliance fleet must scale out and fail over between healthy instances automatically, and the inspection must be transparent: the application must see the original client IP addresses.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Replace the appliances with AWS Network Firewall and route the internet gateway's ingress traffic through its firewall endpoints
options.explanation: Network Firewall inspects transparently and scales, but it is not the third-party appliance the auditors have approved.

options.text: Put the appliances behind a Network Load Balancer and point the internet gateway's ingress route table at the load balancer
options.explanation: A Network Load Balancer is not a valid route table target, so traffic cannot be steered through it as a next hop.

options.text: Register the appliances with a Gateway Load Balancer and route the internet gateway's ingress traffic to its VPC endpoints
Disable source/destination checks on one appliance per Availability Zone and route ingress traffic to its network interface
options.explanation: Routing to an appliance's interface is transparent, but nothing scales the fleet or moves traffic off a failed instance.

explanation: A Gateway Load Balancer is a layer 3 transparent gateway that distributes traffic to registered virtual appliances over GENEVE, health checks them and keeps flows sticky; Gateway Load Balancer endpoints can be used as next hops in route tables, including the internet gateway's ingress route table, so packets keep their original addresses. Network Firewall is a different product, an NLB cannot be a route target, and a single appliance per AZ neither scales nor fails over. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/gateway/introduction.html

prompt:
A company connects its data center to a VPC through a 1 Gbps AWS Direct Connect hosted connection from a partner, using a private virtual interface. A new regulation requires all traffic between the data center and the VPC to be encrypted in transit. The company wants to keep using the Direct Connect link rather than send the traffic over the internet.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable MACsec on the hosted connection and configure a CKN/CAK pair on the data center's edge router
options.explanation: MACsec is supported on certain 10, 100 and 400 Gbps dedicated connections, not on hosted connections.

options.text: Keep the private virtual interface as it is, because Direct Connect traffic travels over a private circuit
options.explanation: Direct Connect does not encrypt traffic in transit by default; a private circuit is isolated, not encrypted.

options.text: Create an AWS Client VPN endpoint in the VPC and have the data center servers connect to it as VPN clients
options.explanation: Client VPN is built for individual users' devices, not for routing a whole data center network over the link.

options.text: Run an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection over the Direct Connect link to get an IPsec-encrypted tunnel

explanation: Direct Connect does not encrypt traffic in transit by default. Combining it with AWS Site-to-Site VPN, for example over a public or transit virtual interface, gives an IPsec-encrypted private connection that still uses the Direct Connect link. MACsec would encrypt at layer 2, but it needs a supported dedicated connection, and Client VPN is for individual users. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/encryption-in-transit.html

prompt:
A company encrypts application data with a symmetric customer managed AWS KMS key whose key material was generated by AWS KMS. A new security standard requires the key material to be replaced every year. Data encrypted before each change must remain readable, and the application must keep using the same key ID.

Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Import new key material into the existing KMS key once a year and keep the earlier material for decryption
options.explanation: Key material can be imported only into keys created with an EXTERNAL origin; this key's material was generated by KMS.

options.text: Turn on automatic key rotation for the customer managed key with a rotation period of 365 days
Switch the application to the AWS managed key for the service, which KMS rotates every year
options.explanation: An AWS managed key has a different key ID and a key policy the company cannot edit, so the application and its controls would change.

options.text: Create a new customer managed key each year and point the application's key alias at the new key
options.explanation: A new key has a new key ID, and old ciphertext still needs the old key kept and tracked, which adds work every year.

explanation: Automatic key rotation on a customer managed key creates new key material on the rotation period (365 days by default) while the key ID stays the same, and KMS transparently uses the older material to decrypt data encrypted before the rotation. Importing material only works for EXTERNAL-origin keys, an AWS managed key changes the key ID and policy, and a new key each year means tracking several keys. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotate-keys.html

prompt:
A company stores customer records in an Amazon S3 bucket. A security review finds that some internal tools still call the bucket over plain HTTP. The company requires that every request to the bucket made over plain HTTP is rejected.

Which solution meets this requirement?

options.text: Set the bucket's default encryption to server-side encryption with an AWS KMS customer managed key
options.explanation: Default encryption protects objects at rest; it does not stop a client from sending requests over HTTP.

options.text: Turn on all four S3 Block Public Access settings for the bucket and for the account
options.explanation: Block Public Access stops public grants through ACLs and policies; it does not look at the transport a request uses.

options.text: Turn on the s3-bucket-ssl-requests-only AWS Config managed rule for the bucket
options.explanation: The Config rule reports whether the bucket policy requires HTTPS; it does not reject any request by itself.

options.text: Add a bucket policy statement that denies all S3 actions when aws:SecureTransport is false

explanation: A bucket policy Deny statement with the condition aws:SecureTransport equal to false rejects every request made over HTTP, whoever sends it, because an explicit deny overrides any allow. Default encryption is about data at rest, Block Public Access is about public grants, and the Config rule only detects a missing policy. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/security-best-practices.html

prompt:
Developers in a company's AWS account launch Amazon EC2 instances in the eu-west-1 Region from many different templates and scripts. The security team requires that every new Amazon EBS volume created in that Region is encrypted at rest, even when a developer leaves the encryption option off.

Which solution meets this requirement?

options.text: Turn on EBS encryption by default for the account in eu-west-1 and choose the KMS key to use
Turn on the encrypted-volumes AWS Config managed rule in eu-west-1 for all attached volumes
options.explanation: The Config rule reports unencrypted volumes after they exist; it does not make new volumes encrypted.

options.text: Create an Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policy that copies each volume's snapshots with encryption
options.explanation: Encrypted snapshot copies protect backups, but the volumes the instances use stay unencrypted.

options.text: Turn on automatic key rotation for the aws/ebs AWS managed key in eu-west-1
options.explanation: Rotation changes key material and is not configurable for AWS managed keys; it does not cause volumes to be encrypted.

explanation: EBS encryption by default is a per-Region account setting: once on, every new volume and snapshot copy in that Region is encrypted with the default KMS key, whatever the launch request says. A Config rule only detects, snapshot copies leave the live volumes unencrypted, and key rotation does not turn encryption on. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/encryption-by-default.html

prompt:
A web application stores customer invoices as objects in a private Amazon S3 bucket. Customers sign in to the application and have no AWS identities. When a customer asks for an invoice, the application must give the customer a link that downloads only that invoice and stops working after 1 hour. The bucket must stay private.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Grant public-read on each invoice object through an object ACL and remove the grant after 1 hour
options.explanation: A public-read grant makes the object public to anyone with the URL, which breaks the requirement that the bucket stays private.

options.text: Create an IAM user for each customer with a policy that allows s3:GetObject on that customer's invoices
options.explanation: Customers do not have AWS identities, and managing an IAM user per customer does not produce a 1-hour link.

options.text: Have the application generate an S3 presigned URL for the invoice object with a 1-hour expiration
Add a bucket policy that allows s3:GetObject when the aws:Referer header matches the application's domain
options.explanation: The Referer header is set by the client and easily forged, and the grant has no expiry for each link.

explanation: A presigned URL is signed with the application's credentials and grants time-limited permission to download one object, so the customer needs no AWS identity and the bucket stays private. Object ACL grants make data public, IAM users per customer do not fit outside users, and a Referer condition can be spoofed and never expires. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ShareObjectPreSignedURL.html

prompt:
A company runs workloads on Amazon RDS, Amazon EBS, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon EFS. Each team configures its own backups today, and auditors cannot see a single policy. The company wants daily backups kept for 35 days for every resource tagged backup=daily, defined and monitored in one place.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policies that target the backup=daily tag with a daily schedule
options.explanation: Data Lifecycle Manager manages EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs only, so RDS, DynamoDB, and EFS are not covered.

options.text: Create an AWS Backup plan with a daily rule and 35-day retention, and assign resources by the backup=daily tag
Set 35-day automated backups on RDS, point-in-time recovery on DynamoDB, and snapshots for EBS and EFS
options.explanation: These are separate per-service settings with no single policy or view, which is the problem the auditors raised.

options.text: Use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery to replicate the tagged resources to a recovery Region every day
options.explanation: Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates servers for failover; it does not back up DynamoDB tables or EFS file systems.

explanation: An AWS Backup plan is a single policy that sets the schedule and retention, and tag-based resource assignment pulls in every supported resource tagged backup=daily, across RDS, EBS, DynamoDB, and EFS. Data Lifecycle Manager covers only EBS, per-service settings leave no central policy, and Elastic Disaster Recovery is for server replication. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-backup/latest/devguide/about-backup-plans.html

prompt:
Auditors ask a company to show which Amazon EBS volumes attached to its EC2 instances are unencrypted, including volumes created years ago, and to keep that report current as volumes change. Remediation will be handled later by each team.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Turn on EBS encryption by default in each Region where the company runs instances
options.explanation: Encryption by default applies only to new volumes and does not report on volumes that already exist.

options.text: Create an AWS CloudTrail trail that records CreateVolume calls and send the events to Amazon CloudWatch Logs
options.explanation: CloudTrail records API calls made from now on; it does not evaluate the current encryption state of existing volumes.

options.text: Turn on Amazon Inspector scanning for the EC2 instances and review the findings for each volume
options.explanation: Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities and network exposure, not for the encryption setting of EBS volumes.

options.text: Turn on AWS Config and add the encrypted-volumes managed rule to flag noncompliant volumes

explanation: AWS Config records resource configurations, and the encrypted-volumes managed rule marks every attached EBS volume that is unencrypted as NON_COMPLIANT, re-evaluating as volumes change. Encryption by default affects only new volumes, CloudTrail logs API calls rather than evaluating state, and Inspector looks for vulnerabilities. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/encrypted-volumes.html

prompt:
Analysts save reports to an Amazon S3 bucket and sometimes overwrite or delete a file by mistake. The company wants to restore any earlier copy of a report, including one replaced minutes ago. Analysts must still be able to replace and delete reports as part of their normal work.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket and restore the earlier object version when a mistake happens
Enable S3 Object Lock in governance mode on the bucket with a default retention period of 30 days
options.explanation: Object Lock retention stops analysts from deleting or overwriting locked versions, which blocks their normal work.

options.text: Enable S3 server access logging on the bucket and review the logs when a report is lost
options.explanation: Access logs show who overwrote or deleted an object, but they hold no copy of the data to restore.

options.text: Add an S3 Lifecycle rule that moves reports to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 1 day
options.explanation: Changing the storage class lowers cost but keeps no earlier copies when a report is overwritten or deleted.

explanation: With S3 Versioning, an overwrite creates a new version and a delete adds a delete marker, so every earlier version stays in the bucket and can be restored at once, while analysts can still replace and delete files. Object Lock blocks those normal deletes, access logs keep no data, and a lifecycle transition keeps no older copies. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Versioning.html

prompt:
A company runs an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance that was created without storage encryption. A new policy requires the database, its backups, and its snapshots to be encrypted with a customer managed AWS KMS key. A short maintenance window for cutover is acceptable.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Modify the DB instance to turn on storage encryption with the customer managed key and apply the change in the next window
options.explanation: RDS encryption can be set only when an instance is created; an existing unencrypted instance cannot be modified to encrypt it.

options.text: Create a read replica encrypted with the customer managed key, then promote the replica during the maintenance window
options.explanation: RDS does not allow an encrypted read replica of an unencrypted DB instance.

options.text: Take a manual snapshot, copy it with encryption using the customer managed key, and restore a new instance from the copy
Turn on EBS encryption by default with the customer managed key in the Region, then reboot the DB instance
options.explanation: EBS encryption by default affects new EC2 volumes only and does not change the storage of an existing RDS instance.

explanation: Encryption cannot be turned on for an existing RDS instance, but an unencrypted snapshot can be copied as an encrypted snapshot under a chosen KMS key, and an instance restored from it is encrypted along with its backups and snapshots. Modifying the instance is not supported, encrypted replicas of unencrypted sources are not allowed, and EBS defaults do not touch RDS storage. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Overview.Encryption.html

prompt:
A company runs an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL 14 DB instance that uses the default DB parameter group. Several client applications, some owned by other teams, connect to it. Compliance requires the database itself to refuse any connection made without SSL/TLS, regardless of how each client is configured.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a custom DB parameter group with rds.force_ssl set to 1, associate it with the instance, and reboot
Set rds.force_ssl to 1 in the default DB parameter group that the instance already uses
options.explanation: Default DB parameter groups cannot be modified; changing a parameter requires a custom parameter group.

options.text: Distribute the RDS certificate bundle and set sslmode=verify-full in every client's connection string
options.explanation: This secures the clients that adopt it, but the server still accepts plain connections from any client that does not.

options.text: Turn on storage encryption with a customer managed AWS KMS key by restoring from an encrypted snapshot copy
options.explanation: Storage encryption protects data at rest and does nothing to require TLS on client connections.

explanation: On RDS for PostgreSQL 14, rds.force_ssl defaults to 0; setting it to 1 makes the server reject non-SSL connections. Default parameter groups cannot be edited, so the value goes in a custom parameter group, which a running instance picks up after a reboot. Client-side sslmode settings do not bind other clients, and storage encryption covers data at rest only. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/PostgreSQL.Concepts.General.SSL.html

prompt:
A company is moving a document-signing application to AWS. The application calls a hardware security module through the PKCS #11 API. Regulators require the signing keys to live in single-tenant, FIPS-validated HSMs, with the company managing the HSM users and AWS having no access to the key material.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an asymmetric AWS KMS customer managed key with imported key material and sign through the KMS API
options.explanation: Imported material still lives in multi-tenant KMS HSMs operated by AWS, and KMS does not offer a PKCS #11 interface.

options.text: Create an asymmetric AWS KMS customer managed key whose key policy allows only the application's IAM role
options.explanation: A key policy limits who can use the key, but the key still sits in shared KMS HSMs managed by AWS.

options.text: Store the private signing key in AWS Secrets Manager, encrypted with a customer managed KMS key
options.explanation: The application would load the key into memory and sign in software, so the key is no longer held in an HSM.

options.text: Deploy an AWS CloudHSM cluster across two Availability Zones and use its PKCS #11 library in the app

explanation: AWS CloudHSM provides single-tenant, FIPS-validated HSMs in the company's VPC; the company creates and manages the HSM users, the data plane is not visible to AWS, and its client SDK supports PKCS #11 so the application changes little. KMS keys, whether imported or tightly scoped, sit in AWS-operated multi-tenant HSMs, and Secrets Manager would move signing into software. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudhsm/latest/userguide/introduction.html

prompt:
A company serves www.example.com from an Application Load Balancer in eu-west-1 that uses an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate issued in eu-west-1. The company is adding an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the ALB with www.example.com as an alternate domain name. The certificate is missing from the list when the team edits the distribution. Certificates must keep renewing automatically.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Request a new ACM certificate for www.example.com in eu-west-1 with DNS validation and attach it to the distribution
options.explanation: CloudFront only uses ACM certificates from us-east-1, so a second eu-west-1 certificate still cannot be selected.

options.text: Request an ACM certificate for www.example.com in us-east-1 with DNS validation and attach it to the distribution
Attach the existing eu-west-1 certificate to the distribution by passing its ARN through the CloudFront API
options.explanation: The Region requirement applies to the API as well; CloudFront rejects ACM certificates outside us-east-1.

options.text: Buy a certificate from a third-party CA and upload it to the IAM certificate store for use with CloudFront
options.explanation: CloudFront can use an IAM-stored certificate, but it would not renew automatically as the requirement demands.

explanation: To use an ACM certificate between viewers and CloudFront, the certificate must be requested or imported in US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1; a DNS-validated ACM certificate there renews automatically. The ALB can keep its eu-west-1 certificate for the CloudFront-to-origin leg. Certificates in eu-west-1 cannot be attached to a distribution by any route, and a third-party certificate in IAM needs manual renewal. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/cnames-and-https-requirements.html

prompt:
A company uses an organization trail in AWS CloudTrail. During an investigation, auditors must be able to prove that each delivered log file is exactly as CloudTrail wrote it and that none were deleted. Administrators in the workload accounts must also be unable to remove or overwrite the stored logs.

Which TWO actions together meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Turn on log file integrity validation for the trail so that CloudTrail delivers signed digest files
Encrypt the log files with SSE-KMS using a customer managed key that only the security team can use
options.explanation: KMS encryption controls who can read the logs; it gives no proof that a file was not altered or removed.

options.text: Send the trail to Amazon CloudWatch Logs as well and keep the log group for 1 year
options.explanation: A second copy helps searching, but it proves nothing about the S3 files and can itself be deleted by admins.

options.text: Deliver the logs to a bucket in a separate log archive account with S3 Object Lock in compliance mode
Turn on S3 server access logging for the log bucket and store the access logs in a second bucket
options.explanation: Access logs record who touched the files after the fact; they neither prevent deletion nor prove integrity.

explanation: Log file integrity validation makes CloudTrail deliver hourly digest files that hold SHA-256 hashes of each log file and are signed with RSA, so a modified or deleted file is detected. Storing the logs in a separate log archive account with Object Lock compliance mode keeps workload-account administrators from deleting or overwriting them. KMS encryption, a CloudWatch Logs copy, and access logging each leave one of the two requirements unmet. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro.html

prompt:
A company created an Amazon S3 bucket years ago with the Object writer ownership setting. Partner accounts upload files to it without specifying any ACL, so the partners own those objects and the company's bucket policy has no effect on them. The company wants to own every object in the bucket, including those already uploaded, and to control access only through policies. Partners will keep their upload code unchanged.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Change the bucket's S3 Object Ownership setting to Bucket owner preferred
options.explanation: Bucket owner preferred applies only to new uploads that include the bucket-owner-full-control ACL, which partners do not send.

options.text: Add a bucket policy that denies s3:PutObject unless the request includes the bucket-owner-full-control ACL
options.explanation: This forces partners to change their uploads and leaves ACLs active and existing partner-owned objects untouched.

options.text: Change the bucket's S3 Object Ownership setting to Bucket owner enforced
Turn on all four S3 Block Public Access settings for the bucket to neutralise object ACLs
options.explanation: Block Public Access ignores only public ACL grants; partners would still own their objects and private ACLs still apply.

explanation: Bucket owner enforced disables ACLs and makes the bucket owner the owner of every new and existing object, so access is decided by policies alone, and uploads without an ACL keep working. Bucket owner preferred needs the bucket-owner-full-control ACL on each new upload and does not change existing objects, a policy requiring that ACL forces partner code changes, and Block Public Access does not change ownership. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/about-object-ownership.html

prompt:
A company uses AWS Backup to protect production databases and volumes. After a ransomware incident at a peer, the board requires that no one, including an attacker holding the production account's root user, can delete a backup before its 35-day retention ends, and that a copy of every backup is held outside the production account.

Which TWO actions together meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Apply AWS Backup Vault Lock in governance mode to the backup vaults with a 35-day minimum retention
options.explanation: In governance mode, any principal with sufficient IAM permissions, such as the root user, can remove the lock and delete backups.

options.text: Apply AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode to the backup vaults and let the grace time expire
Add a copy rule to the backup plan that copies each recovery point to a vault in another Region
options.explanation: A vault in another Region of the same account is still controlled by whoever holds that account's root user.

options.text: Attach a vault access policy that denies backup:DeleteRecoveryPoint to every principal in the account
options.explanation: An administrator or root user of the account can edit or delete the vault access policy and then delete the backups.

options.text: Add a copy rule to the backup plan that copies each recovery point to a vault in a separate account

explanation: Once its grace time ends, a compliance-mode Vault Lock cannot be changed or removed by any user, including the root user, or by AWS, and recovery points cannot be deleted before their retention ends. A copy rule to a vault in a separate account in the organization keeps a copy beyond the reach of the production account. Governance mode can be lifted with IAM permissions, a vault access policy can be edited by an admin, and a cross-Region copy stays in the same account. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-backup/latest/devguide/vault-lock.html

prompt:
A data platform writes and reads millions of small objects per hour in an Amazon S3 bucket encrypted with SSE-KMS and a customer managed key. The AWS KMS bill has grown sharply and some requests fail with KMS throttling errors. The data must stay encrypted under the same customer managed key. The key policy grants decrypt only when the kms:EncryptionContext:aws:s3:arn condition matches the ARN of each object under a prefix.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Switch the bucket's default encryption to the aws/s3 AWS managed key, which does not count against KMS request quotas
options.explanation: S3 still calls KMS for each object with the AWS managed key, and the data would leave the required customer managed key.

options.text: Request a higher KMS cryptographic request quota for the Region and keep the bucket's current encryption settings
options.explanation: A higher quota may ease throttling, but every object request still calls KMS, so the cost keeps growing.

options.text: Switch the bucket's default encryption to DSSE-KMS with the same customer managed key and an S3 Bucket Key
options.explanation: S3 Bucket Keys are not supported with DSSE-KMS, and dual-layer encryption adds work rather than reducing KMS calls.

options.text: Enable an S3 Bucket Key on the bucket and change the key policy condition to match the bucket ARN as encryption context

explanation: An S3 Bucket Key lets S3 keep a short-lived bucket-level key derived from the KMS key and create object data keys from it, cutting KMS requests and cost by up to 99 percent with the same customer managed key. With a Bucket Key, S3 uses the bucket ARN, not the object ARN, as encryption context, so key policy conditions written for object ARNs must be updated or decrypts fail. The AWS managed key still calls KMS per object, a quota increase leaves cost unchanged, and DSSE-KMS does not support Bucket Keys. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/bucket-key.html

prompt:
An application in us-east-1 encrypts records on the client side with the AWS Encryption SDK under a single-Region customer managed KMS key, then stores them in an Amazon DynamoDB global table that replicates to eu-west-1. A standby copy of the application in eu-west-1 must decrypt the records during a us-east-1 outage, without calling KMS in another Region and without re-encrypting each record when it reaches eu-west-1.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a multi-Region primary key in us-east-1, replicate it to eu-west-1, and encrypt records under it
Update the existing key's multi-Region property to true and create a replica of it in eu-west-1
options.explanation: A single-Region key cannot be converted to a multi-Region key; the property is fixed when the key is created.

options.text: Create a key in eu-west-1 with the same alias and a key policy that matches the us-east-1 key
options.explanation: A matching alias and policy do not make two keys share key material, so the eu-west-1 key cannot decrypt the records.

options.text: Grant the eu-west-1 application role kms:Decrypt on the us-east-1 key in that key's key policy
options.explanation: The standby would still call KMS in us-east-1 to decrypt, which fails during the very outage it must survive.

explanation: Related multi-Region keys share key ID and key material, so ciphertext produced under the us-east-1 primary can be decrypted by its eu-west-1 replica locally, with no cross-Region KMS call and no re-encryption. The multi-Region property must be set at creation, so the existing key cannot be converted; a lookalike key has different material; and a cross-Region grant still depends on KMS in us-east-1. Existing records encrypted under the old key need to be re-encrypted under the new key once. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/multi-region-keys-overview.html

prompt:
An order web front end calls a back-end fulfillment service directly. During sales the fulfillment service falls behind and the front end times out, losing orders. The company wants the front end to accept orders immediately, have each order processed by exactly one of a scalable pool of fulfillment workers, and keep orders safe while workers catch up.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Have the front end publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic that the fulfillment workers subscribe to over HTTPS
options.explanation: SNS pushes every message to every subscriber and does not hold orders while workers are busy, so it neither shares work nor buffers it.

options.text: Have the front end send each order to an Amazon SQS queue and have the fulfillment workers poll the queue
Have the front end write each order to an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis list that the fulfillment workers pop from
options.explanation: A cache list can be lost on node failure and has no visibility timeout, so an order a worker crashes on is gone.

options.text: Put an Application Load Balancer in front of the fulfillment workers and scale them on the request count per target
options.explanation: The front end still waits on a synchronous call, so a backlog still turns into timeouts and lost orders.

explanation: An SQS queue decouples the tiers: the front end gets a quick acknowledgement once the message is stored durably, each message goes to one worker at a time, and unprocessed orders wait in the queue while the worker pool scales on queue depth. SNS fans out instead of sharing work, a cache list is not durable, and a load balancer keeps the call synchronous. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html

prompt:
A company runs its customer database on a Single-AZ Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. If the instance's Availability Zone fails, the database must come back automatically on the same endpoint within a few minutes, without losing committed transactions.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a read replica in another Availability Zone and point the application at it if the primary fails
options.explanation: Replication to a read replica is asynchronous and promotion is a manual step that produces a new endpoint.

options.text: Turn on automated backups with a 35-day retention period and restore to the latest restorable time after a failure
options.explanation: A point-in-time restore creates a new instance with a new endpoint, takes longer, and can lose the last few minutes of writes.

options.text: Convert the DB instance to a Multi-AZ deployment with a standby in another Availability Zone
Move the instance to a larger instance class with Provisioned IOPS storage so it recovers faster after an outage
options.explanation: A bigger instance is still a single instance in one Availability Zone; it does not survive that zone failing.

explanation: A Multi-AZ DB instance replicates synchronously to a standby in another Availability Zone and fails over automatically, typically within a couple of minutes, keeping the same DNS endpoint and every committed transaction. A read replica is asynchronous with manual promotion, a restore is slow and lossy, and a larger instance is still one zone. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html

prompt:
A web application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Sometimes the application process hangs: the load balancer marks the instance unhealthy and stops sending it traffic, but the instance keeps running and passing EC2 status checks, so the group never replaces it.

What should a solutions architect do so that hung instances are replaced automatically?

options.text: Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group so it uses the target group's health check results
Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System for each instance with the EC2 recover action
options.explanation: The recover action handles underlying hardware failure, and these instances pass their status checks, so the alarm never fires.

options.text: Keep the default EC2 health checks and raise the load balancer's unhealthy threshold so instances get more time to recover
options.explanation: This only delays the load balancer's verdict; the group still never learns the instance is broken or replaces it.

options.text: Add a target tracking scaling policy on average CPU so the group launches new instances when the hung one stops serving
options.explanation: Scaling adds capacity but leaves the hung instance in the group, and a hung process may not move CPU at all.

explanation: By default an Auto Scaling group judges health only by EC2 status checks. With ELB health checks turned on, an instance that fails the target group's health check is marked unhealthy and replaced. The recover action is for hardware faults, a higher threshold only delays the verdict, and scaling policies add instances without removing the broken one. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-health-checks.html

prompt:
Workers consume messages from an Amazon SQS standard queue with the default 30-second visibility timeout. Processing a message takes up to 2 minutes. The team sees many messages processed two or three times by different workers, which creates duplicate shipments.

Which change fixes the root cause?

options.text: Replace the queue with an SQS FIFO queue with content-based deduplication turned on
options.explanation: FIFO deduplication removes duplicate sends within 5 minutes; a message whose visibility timeout expires mid-processing is still delivered again.

options.text: Turn on long polling by setting the queue's receive message wait time to 20 seconds
options.explanation: Long polling reduces empty receives and cost; it does not stop a message from becoming visible again while it is being processed.

options.text: Add a dead-letter queue with a maximum receive count of 1 so a message is never handled twice
options.explanation: Messages would move to the dead-letter queue on their second receive instead of being processed, so orders would be dropped.

options.text: Set the queue's visibility timeout to longer than the maximum processing time, for example 3 minutes

explanation: While a worker processes a message, the message is hidden for the visibility timeout. At 30 seconds it reappears long before a 2-minute job finishes, and another worker picks it up. Setting the timeout above the longest processing time, or extending it from the worker, stops the redelivery. FIFO deduplication acts on sends, long polling on empty receives, and a receive count of 1 discards work. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html

prompt:
When a customer places an order, three independent systems must act on it: billing, shipping and analytics. Each system runs on its own fleet of EC2 instances, processes at its own pace, and can be offline for hours during maintenance without losing any orders. New systems will be added later without changing the order service.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Publish orders to an SNS topic, subscribe one SQS queue per system, and have each fleet poll its own queue
Send orders to a single Amazon SQS standard queue and have all three fleets poll that queue for new orders
options.explanation: Each SQS message is consumed by only one receiver, so every order would reach just one of the three systems.

options.text: Publish orders to an Amazon SNS topic and subscribe each fleet's HTTPS endpoint behind its own load balancer
options.explanation: SNS retries HTTPS deliveries for a limited time; a fleet that is down for hours of maintenance misses orders.

options.text: Have the order service call each system's API in turn and record failed calls in a DynamoDB table to retry later
options.explanation: The order service has to know every consumer and own the retry logic, so adding a system means changing it.

explanation: SNS-to-SQS fan-out copies each order into a durable queue per system, so each fleet drains its own queue at its own pace and catches up after maintenance; adding a system is one more subscribed queue. A single queue delivers each order to one consumer, HTTPS subscriptions are not a buffer for hours of downtime, and direct calls couple the order service to every consumer. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-sqs-as-subscriber.html

prompt:
A company runs its application in us-east-1 and keeps a scaled-down standby copy in us-west-2 that must not receive traffic in normal operation. If the primary application becomes unhealthy, users must be sent to us-west-2 automatically through the application's DNS name.

Which Amazon Route 53 configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Latency-based routing with one record per Region so each user is sent to the Region with the lowest latency
options.explanation: Latency routing sends users near us-west-2 to the standby during normal operation, which the requirements forbid.

options.text: Multivalue answer routing with both Regions' endpoints so clients pick from the healthy addresses returned
options.explanation: Both Regions are returned and used while healthy, so the scaled-down standby takes live traffic.

options.text: Failover routing with a health-checked us-east-1 record as primary and the us-west-2 record as secondary
Geolocation routing that maps North America to us-east-1 and sets us-west-2 as the default location record
options.explanation: Geolocation picks a Region by where the user is, not by health; users outside North America would land on the standby.

explanation: Failover routing answers with the primary record while its health check passes and switches to the secondary only when it fails, which is exactly active-passive. Latency, multivalue and geolocation routing all send live traffic to the standby in normal operation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/dns-failover-types.html

prompt:
A company needs a disaster recovery plan in a second AWS Region for a business application. The requirements are a recovery point objective (RPO) under 1 minute and a recovery time objective (RTO) of 1 hour, at the lowest ongoing cost.

Which disaster recovery strategy meets these requirements?

options.text: Backup and restore, copying hourly snapshots and backups to the second Region and rebuilding there after a disaster
options.explanation: Hourly backups mean up to an hour of lost data, far beyond an RPO under 1 minute.

options.text: Pilot light, replicating data continuously to the second Region and starting application servers only on recovery
Warm standby, running a scaled-down but fully working copy of the whole stack in the second Region at all times
options.explanation: Warm standby meets both objectives but keeps the whole stack running, so it costs more than the targets require.

options.text: Multi-site active-active, serving production traffic from both Regions at full capacity all the time
options.explanation: Active-active gives near-zero RTO and RPO at the highest cost, well beyond what a 1-hour RTO needs.

explanation: Pilot light keeps the data live in the recovery Region through continuous replication, so the RPO is seconds, while compute stays off until it is needed and is started within tens of minutes, which fits a 1-hour RTO cheaply. Backup and restore cannot meet the RPO, and warm standby and multi-site meet it at a higher running cost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html

prompt:
A global trading platform uses an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster in eu-west-1. Regulators require it to survive the loss of the entire Region with a recovery point objective of seconds and a recovery time objective of minutes, with replication that does not consume the primary database instances' compute.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add Aurora Replicas in all three Availability Zones of eu-west-1 so the cluster fails over automatically to a replica
options.explanation: Aurora Replicas protect against instance and zone failures within eu-west-1, not against losing the whole Region.

options.text: Copy automated cluster snapshots to a second Region every hour and restore the latest snapshot there after a disaster
options.explanation: Hourly snapshot copies give an RPO of up to an hour, and restoring a cluster takes far longer than minutes.

options.text: Use AWS DMS ongoing replication from the cluster into an Amazon RDS for MySQL instance in a second Region
options.explanation: DMS replication reads change logs through database connections, adds lag, and needs a manual cutover to a different engine.

options.text: Convert the cluster to an Aurora global database with a secondary cluster in another Region and fail over to it

explanation: An Aurora global database replicates at the storage layer to secondary Regions, typically with under a second of lag and without using the primary instances' compute, and a secondary cluster can be promoted within minutes. Aurora Replicas stay in one Region, snapshot copies are hours behind, and DMS adds lag and a manual engine switch. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-global-database.html

prompt:
A web application runs on a single large Amazon EC2 instance and keeps user sessions in the instance's memory. When the instance fails, the site goes down and every user is logged out. The company wants the application to tolerate the loss of an instance or an Availability Zone without logging users out.

Which TWO changes together meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Store session data in Amazon ElastiCache or Amazon DynamoDB instead of in instance memory
Turn on sticky sessions on the load balancer so each user keeps returning to the instance that holds the session
options.explanation: Stickiness keeps sessions on one instance, so those users are still logged out when that instance fails.

options.text: Run the instances in an Auto Scaling group across at least two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer
Launch the instances into a cluster placement group so they can share session state over a low-latency network
options.explanation: A cluster placement group packs instances into one Availability Zone, which makes a zone failure take them all down.

options.text: Move to a larger instance type with more memory and turn on EC2 automatic recovery for the instance
options.explanation: Automatic recovery restarts the instance on new hardware, losing in-memory sessions, and one instance in one zone is still a single point of failure.

explanation: Moving sessions to a shared store makes the web tier stateless, so any instance can serve any user, and an Auto Scaling group across Availability Zones behind a load balancer replaces failed instances and survives a zone outage. Sticky sessions and automatic recovery still lose the sessions of a failed instance, and a cluster placement group is confined to one zone. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/elasticache-use-cases.html

prompt:
An insurance claims process has six steps implemented as AWS Lambda functions. Some steps must be retried with backoff on failure, a failure late in the process must run compensating steps for earlier ones, and one step waits for a human adjuster's approval, which can take up to 5 days. The team wants the process state managed by AWS rather than in its own code.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: An AWS Step Functions Express workflow that calls each function and waits for the adjuster's approval with a callback
options.explanation: Express workflows run for at most 5 minutes, so they cannot wait days for an approval.

options.text: A chain of Amazon SQS queues between the functions, with dead-letter queues for failures and a queue for approvals
options.explanation: Queues move messages between steps but nothing tracks the claim's overall state or triggers compensation for earlier steps.

options.text: A coordinator Lambda function that invokes each step in order and sleeps between polls until the adjuster approves
options.explanation: A Lambda function runs for at most 15 minutes, so it cannot wait for a 5-day approval, and the state lives in its code.

options.text: An AWS Step Functions Standard workflow with Retry and Catch on each task and a task token callback for the approval

explanation: Standard workflows can run for up to a year with the state kept by Step Functions; Retry adds backoff, Catch routes failures to compensating states, and the wait-for-task-token pattern pauses until the approval system returns the token. Express workflows stop at 5 minutes, Lambda at 15 minutes, and a chain of queues has no overall state. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/choosing-workflow-type.html

prompt:
A payments service sends account events to Amazon SQS. Events for the same account must be processed in the order they were sent, but events for different accounts are independent. Traffic is growing, and the team needs many consumers processing in parallel.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use an SQS FIFO queue and set the message group ID of each event to the account ID
Use an SQS FIFO queue and set the same message group ID on every event so that all events stay ordered
options.explanation: One message group is processed strictly one message at a time, so consumers cannot work in parallel as traffic grows.

options.text: Use an SQS standard queue with a sequence number attribute on each event and reorder the events in the consumers
options.explanation: Standard queues may deliver out of order and more than once, so consumers must build their own buffering and deduplication.

options.text: Use an Amazon Kinesis data stream with a single shard so that every event is read in the order it was written
options.explanation: One shard keeps order but caps throughput and lets only one reader per consumer process events at a time.

explanation: A FIFO queue keeps strict order within each message group, and different groups can be processed in parallel by different consumers. Using the account ID as the group ID gives per-account order with throughput that grows with the number of accounts. A single group serializes everything, a standard queue pushes ordering into code, and a single shard caps throughput. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/using-messagegroupid-property.html

prompt:
A content management system runs on Linux EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across three Availability Zones. All instances must read and write the same set of uploaded files at the same time, and the files must stay available if an Availability Zone fails.

Which storage solution meets these requirements?

options.text: An Amazon EBS Provisioned IOPS volume with Multi-Attach enabled, attached to every instance
options.explanation: Multi-Attach works only within one Availability Zone and needs a cluster-aware file system, so it cannot span the group.

options.text: An Amazon EFS Regional file system, mounted on every instance over NFS
Instance store volumes on each instance, kept in step with a sync job that runs every minute
options.explanation: Instance store data is lost when an instance stops or fails, and a sync job leaves the copies out of step.

options.text: An Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system, mounted on every instance over SMB
options.explanation: FSx for Windows File Server serves SMB for Windows workloads; Linux NFS clients in an Auto Scaling group are what EFS is built for.

explanation: Amazon EFS is a managed NFS file system that many Linux instances in different Availability Zones can mount at the same time, and a Regional file system stores data redundantly across zones. EBS Multi-Attach is limited to one zone, instance store is ephemeral, and FSx for Windows File Server targets Windows SMB clients. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/whatisefs.html

prompt:
A retail application stores shopping carts in an Amazon DynamoDB table in one Region. The company wants users in a second Region to write to a local copy of the table, both copies to keep working if either Region fails, and the ability to restore the table to any second in the last 35 days after an accidental bulk delete.

Which TWO features together meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) clusters in both Regions in front of the table
options.explanation: DAX caches reads in front of one table; it does not replicate writes to another Region or keep serving if that Region fails.

options.text: DynamoDB global tables with a replica in the second Region
On-demand capacity mode on the table in both Regions
options.explanation: On-demand mode changes how throughput is billed and scaled; it adds no replica and no restore capability.

options.text: Point-in-time recovery turned on for the table
A scheduled daily export of the table to Amazon S3
options.explanation: Daily exports allow recovery only to the time of the last export, not to any second in the last 35 days.

explanation: Global tables replicate a table across Regions with every replica accepting reads and writes, so each Region keeps working if the other fails. Point-in-time recovery keeps continuous backups and restores the table to any second in the last 35 days. DAX is a read cache, on-demand mode is a billing choice, and daily exports cannot reach an arbitrary second. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GlobalTables.html

prompt:
A company runs an HTTPS application behind Application Load Balancers in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Enterprise customers allow outbound traffic only to IP addresses on an allow list and will accept exactly two static IP addresses. If one Region fails, traffic must move to the other within a minute, regardless of client DNS caching.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Assign Elastic IP addresses to both load balancers and use Route 53 failover routing between the two Regions

options.explanation: SNS pushes every message to every subscribed instance and holds nothing back for a free worker.

options.text: Put the instances behind a Network Load Balancer and send the S3 event notifications to it
options.explanation: S3 event notifications go to SNS, SQS, Lambda or EventBridge, not to a load balancer, and a load balancer holds no backlog.

explanation: An SQS queue holds each upload durably until a worker receives and deletes it, so a failed instance's message simply becomes visible again for another worker. Scaling on backlog per instance (visible messages divided by running instances) against how many messages one instance can work through in the acceptable time grows the fleet with the waiting work. CPU doesn't measure the backlog, SNS over HTTP pushes every message to every instance, and S3 can't send events to a load balancer. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-using-sqs-queue.html

A company is moving a Windows document management application to Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. The instances must share files over SMB, enforce Windows NTFS permissions tied to the company's Active Directory, and keep the share available if one Availability Zone fails.

Which storage solution meets these requirements?

options.text: An Amazon EFS Regional file system mounted on every instance
options.explanation: EFS serves NFS to Linux clients; it offers no SMB shares or Windows NTFS permissions.

options.text: An Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach, attached to each instance and formatted with Windows NTFS
options.explanation: Multi-Attach works only within the volume's own Availability Zone, and NTFS isn't a cluster file system, so concurrent writers would corrupt it.

options.text: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server with a Multi-AZ file system joined to the directory
Amazon FSx for Lustre with a persistent file system linked to an S3 bucket
options.explanation: FSx for Lustre is a high-performance file system for Linux clients, with no SMB or Active Directory support.

explanation: FSx for Windows File Server provides native SMB shares with NTFS permissions and Active Directory integration, and a Multi-AZ deployment keeps a standby file server in a second Availability Zone that takes over automatically. EFS serves NFS to Linux clients, EBS Multi-Attach stays inside one Availability Zone, and FSx for Lustre is a Linux high-performance file system. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/WindowsGuide/high-availability-multiAZ.html

prompt:
A gaming leaderboard reads player profiles from an Amazon DynamoDB table. Reads concentrate on a small set of popular profiles, eventually consistent reads are acceptable, and the product team now needs read latency in microseconds rather than single-digit milliseconds. The developers want to change as little code as possible.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Switch the table from provisioned capacity to on-demand capacity mode
options.explanation: Capacity mode changes how throughput is provisioned and billed; reads still take milliseconds.

options.text: Put a DAX cluster in front of the table and use the DAX client in place of the DynamoDB client
Add a global secondary index on the profile attributes the leaderboard reads
options.explanation: An index changes which queries are possible, not how fast a read returns.

options.text: Add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster and write cache-aside logic around each table read
options.explanation: ElastiCache can be as fast, but cache-aside logic has to be written around every read, which is far more code.

explanation: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory cache that is API-compatible with DynamoDB, so swapping the client is the only code change, and eventually consistent reads of hot items come back from its item cache in microseconds. On-demand mode changes how capacity is billed, a GSI changes what you can query, and ElastiCache needs caching logic written around every read. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DAX.html

A company runs 25 microservices on a self-managed Kubernetes cluster in its data center and deploys them with Helm charts. It is moving them to AWS and wants to keep its Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts unchanged, stop operating the control plane, and stop sizing, patching or scaling worker nodes. None of the services uses DaemonSets or privileged containers.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Amazon EKS with managed node groups that use the EKS-optimized AMI
options.explanation: Managed node groups automate node provisioning, but the team still picks instance types, starts AMI updates and scales the nodes.

options.text: Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate, with task definitions converted from the manifests
options.explanation: ECS doesn't run Kubernetes manifests or Helm charts, so every service would have to be redefined as an ECS task definition.

options.text: Amazon EKS with Fargate profiles that select the services' namespaces
Kubernetes on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group, built with kOps
options.explanation: kOps installs Kubernetes on EC2, but the team keeps running the control plane and patching the nodes.

explanation: EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane for you, so the existing manifests and Helm charts deploy unchanged, and a Fargate profile runs the pods of matching namespaces on right-sized compute that AWS provisions and patches, with no nodes to manage. Fargate's limits, such as no DaemonSets or privileged containers, don't affect these services. EKS Auto Mode, which also manages the nodes, would be another fit but isn't offered here. Managed node groups still leave node sizing and AMI updates to the team, ECS needs the manifests rewritten, and kOps leaves the control plane with the team. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/fargate.html

prompt:
A trading platform publishes order events that three downstream systems (settlement, risk and audit) must each process in the exact order they were published for a given account, with duplicates removed. Each system must consume from its own queue so it can scale and retry independently, and adding a fourth system later should need no change to the publisher.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: An Amazon SNS standard topic with an SQS FIFO queue subscribed for each system
options.explanation: An SQS FIFO queue can subscribe only to an SNS FIFO topic, and a standard topic doesn't preserve publishing order.

options.text: One SQS FIFO queue per system, with the publisher sending each event to all of the queues
options.explanation: Order holds, but the publisher has to know every queue, so adding a fourth system means changing the publisher.

options.text: An Amazon EventBridge rule per system that targets that system's SQS FIFO queue
options.explanation: EventBridge doesn't keep events in publishing order, so a queue could receive an account's events out of sequence.

options.text: An Amazon SNS FIFO topic fanning out to an SQS FIFO queue per system, grouped by account ID

explanation: An SNS FIFO topic orders messages within each message group and deduplicates them, and it fans out to SQS FIFO queues that keep that order, so every system gets each account's events in sequence on its own queue, and a new system only adds a subscription. A standard topic can't deliver to FIFO queues, publishing to each queue couples the publisher to every consumer, and EventBridge doesn't keep events in publishing order. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-fifo-topics.html

prompt:
A company must reprocess 8 million JSON files in an Amazon S3 bucket with an existing AWS Lambda function, one file per invocation. It wants up to 1,000 files processed in parallel, a record of which files failed so it can rerun only those, and the run to keep going as long as no more than 1% of files fail. The team wants to write as little orchestration code as possible.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: An AWS Step Functions Distributed Map state over the bucket's objects with a tolerated failure percentage of 1
An AWS Step Functions Inline Map state over the object list with MaxConcurrency set to 1,000
options.explanation: Inline Map runs at most 40 iterations at a time inside one execution, whose 25,000-event history can't hold 8 million items.

options.text: A script on an EC2 instance that lists the bucket and invokes the function asynchronously per key
options.explanation: The script is exactly the orchestration code the team wants to avoid, and it has to track concurrency and failures itself.

options.text: An AWS Batch array job with one child job per file that runs the function's code in a container
options.explanation: Array jobs are limited to 10,000 child jobs, and the function's code would have to be repackaged as a Batch job.

explanation: A Distributed Map state reads S3 objects or an inventory and runs each item as a child workflow execution, with up to 10,000 in parallel; MaxConcurrency caps it at 1,000, a tolerated failure percentage fails the run only past 1%, and ResultWriter exports the failed items to S3 for a rerun. Inline Map runs at most 40 iterations at a time within one execution's history limit, a script is the orchestration code the team wants to avoid, and Batch array jobs stop at 10,000 children. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-map-distributed.html

prompt:
An Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster has a writer and four Aurora Replicas: two db.r6g.large replicas for the customer-facing application's reads and two db.r6g.4xlarge replicas for analysts' heavy queries. The two read workloads must never run on the same replica. Aurora Auto Scaling adds replicas when application reads grow, and those new replicas must serve application reads only.

Which configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Send analytics to a custom endpoint of the two 4xlarge replicas and app reads to one with them on its exclusion list
Send both workloads to the reader endpoint and give the 4xlarge replicas a lower failover priority
options.explanation: The reader endpoint spreads connections across every replica, and promotion tiers only decide which replica becomes the writer.

options.text: Send analytics to the reader endpoint and the application's reads to the cluster endpoint
options.explanation: The cluster endpoint is the writer, and the reader endpoint would spread analytics across the application's replicas.

options.text: Send analytics to the 4xlarge replicas' instance endpoints and the application's reads to the reader endpoint
options.explanation: The reader endpoint includes the 4xlarge replicas, so application reads would land on the analytics instances.

explanation: Custom endpoints load-balance across a chosen set of instances: one with the two 4xlarge replicas as static members serves analytics, and one defined by an exclusion list (every instance but those two) automatically includes replicas added later, such as those from Aurora Auto Scaling. The reader endpoint spreads connections across every replica, failover tiers only set promotion order, the cluster endpoint is the writer, and instance endpoints still leave the reader endpoint mixing the workloads. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Endpoints.Custom.Considerations.html

prompt:
A company stores engineering drawings in an Amazon S3 bucket in eu-west-1. A new policy requires a copy of each new object in a second AWS Region, kept up to date automatically, so the drawings stay available if eu-west-1 becomes unavailable.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Turn on S3 Same-Region Replication to a second bucket in eu-west-1
options.explanation: Same-Region Replication keeps the copy in eu-west-1, so it is lost along with the Region.

options.text: Rely on the S3 Standard storage class, which stores objects across several Availability Zones
options.explanation: S3 Standard spreads data across Availability Zones within one Region; it doesn't protect against losing the Region.

options.text: Turn on S3 Versioning and S3 Cross-Region Replication to a bucket in another Region
Create an AWS Backup plan that backs up the bucket nightly to a vault in eu-west-1
options.explanation: Nightly backups lag up to a day behind, and a vault in the same Region fails with it.

explanation: Cross-Region Replication copies new objects asynchronously to a bucket in a different Region and needs Versioning on both buckets, so a current copy survives the loss of eu-west-1. Same-Region Replication and S3 Standard's multi-AZ storage both stay inside the Region, and nightly backups in the same Region are neither current nor out of the Region. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/replication.html

prompt:
An application runs on four Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. All four instances run in subnets in one Availability Zone, and during an outage of that zone last month the application was down for two hours.

Which change BEST improves the application's availability?

options.text: Replace the instances with a larger instance type in the same subnets
options.explanation: Bigger instances still sit in the one Availability Zone, so a zone outage takes them all down.

options.text: Launch the instances in a spread placement group within the Availability Zone
options.explanation: A spread placement group separates instances onto different racks, but they all stay in the failing zone.

options.text: Take hourly EBS snapshots of each instance so it can be relaunched after an outage
options.explanation: Snapshots speed up a rebuild after the outage; the application is still down while the zone is.

options.text: Add subnets in two more Availability Zones to the group and enable those zones on the load balancer

explanation: With subnets in several Availability Zones, the Auto Scaling group balances instances across them and launches replacements in healthy zones, and the load balancer routes only to healthy targets in its enabled zones, so losing one zone leaves the application running. Larger instances and a spread placement group stay inside the failing zone, and snapshots shorten recovery without avoiding the outage. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-availability-zone-balanced.html

prompt:
A VPC has private subnets in three Availability Zones. All of them send internet-bound traffic through one zonal NAT gateway in the public subnet of AZ A. The company wants instances in AZ B and AZ C to keep outbound internet access if AZ A fails, and it wants to keep using zonal NAT gateways.

Which TWO actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a second Elastic IP address to the existing NAT gateway
options.explanation: More addresses give the gateway more connections, but it still lives only in AZ A.

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in each Availability Zone
Attach an egress-only internet gateway and route the private subnets' IPv4 traffic to it
options.explanation: An egress-only internet gateway carries IPv6 traffic only, so IPv4 instances get no outbound path through it.

options.text: Give each zone's private subnets a route table that points to the NAT gateway in the same zone
Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance managed by an Auto Scaling group of size one
options.explanation: A replacement NAT instance gets a new ID, and the route tables keep pointing at the old one until someone updates them.

explanation: A zonal NAT gateway is redundant only within its own Availability Zone, so a zone-independent design puts a NAT gateway in each zone and gives each zone's private subnets a route table that uses the local gateway. Extra addresses leave the gateway in AZ A, an egress-only internet gateway carries only IPv6, and a NAT instance replaced by Auto Scaling comes back with an ID the route tables don't point to. A regional NAT gateway, which expands across zones by itself, is the alternative for a team willing to change gateway type. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/nat-gateway-basics.html

prompt:
A company's internal wiki runs on one Amazon EC2 instance with an Amazon RDS database in us-east-1. If the Region fails, the business accepts losing up to 24 hours of changes and waiting up to 24 hours for the wiki to come back. The company wants the lowest-cost disaster recovery strategy that meets these objectives.

Which strategy should a solutions architect choose?

options.text: Backup and restore, copying daily backups to a second Region and rebuilding from them
Pilot light, replicating the database continuously to a second Region
options.explanation: Continuous replication buys an RPO of seconds and keeps a database running in the second Region, which a 24-hour RPO doesn't need.

options.text: Warm standby, keeping a scaled-down copy of the wiki running in a second Region
options.explanation: A running copy reaches an RTO of minutes and costs compute all the time, far beyond a 24-hour objective.

options.text: Multi-site active/active, serving users from both Regions at once
options.explanation: Running full capacity in two Regions is the most expensive strategy and meets objectives far tighter than 24 hours.

explanation: With an RPO and RTO of 24 hours, backup and restore is enough: copy daily backups to another Region and rebuild there, ideally with infrastructure as code, after a disaster, paying only for backup storage and copies. Pilot light, warm standby and active/active keep resources running in the second Region to reach RPOs and RTOs of minutes or less, which this wiki doesn't need. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html

prompt:
A company runs the same stateless API behind Application Load Balancers in us-east-1 and ap-southeast-2. Both Regions should serve traffic at all times, each user should reach the Region that gives them the lowest latency, and if one Region's API becomes unhealthy its users should go to the other Region.

Which Amazon Route 53 configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Failover records with us-east-1 as the primary and ap-southeast-2 as the secondary
options.explanation: Failover routing sends everyone to the primary while it is healthy, so ap-southeast-2 sits idle.

options.text: Geolocation records that map each continent to one of the two Regions
options.explanation: Geolocation routes by where the user is rather than by measured latency, so a user isn't sent to the faster Region.

options.text: Weighted records that give both load balancers a weight of 50
options.explanation: Equal weights split users evenly between the Regions regardless of which one is closer to them.
