options.text: Latency records for both load balancers, with health checks evaluated on each record

explanation: Latency-based records send each user to the Region with the lowest latency for them, so both Regions serve traffic, and with health checks (or Evaluate Target Health on alias records) Route 53 stops returning an unhealthy Region's record, so its users go to the other. Failover routing keeps the second Region idle, geolocation routes by location rather than latency, and equal weights ignore where users are. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-policy-latency.html

prompt:
A request to an online store passes through Amazon API Gateway, three AWS Lambda functions and an Amazon DynamoDB table. Some checkout requests take 8 seconds instead of 300 ms, and the team can't tell which component adds the delay. It wants an end-to-end view of individual requests showing the time spent in each service.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a CloudWatch dashboard with the Duration metric of each Lambda function
options.explanation: Duration shows each function's statistics in aggregate, so it can't tie one slow checkout to the call that took the time.

options.text: Turn on AWS X-Ray active tracing for API Gateway and the functions and examine the trace map
Turn on AWS CloudTrail data events for the Lambda functions and the DynamoDB table
options.explanation: CloudTrail records who called which API and when, not how long each hop of a request took.

options.text: Publish VPC Flow Logs for the functions' VPC to Amazon CloudWatch Logs
options.explanation: Flow logs record network connections and bytes, with no view of a request across services.

explanation: X-Ray records a trace for each request as it passes through API Gateway, Lambda and the SDK calls to DynamoDB, and the trace map and timeline show how long each service took and where errors occur. Duration metrics are aggregates, CloudTrail records API activity for auditing, and Flow Logs record network flows with no request timing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/xray/latest/devguide/aws-xray.html

prompt:
A company runs a self-managed application on Amazon EC2 with its data on Amazon EBS volumes. It wants a daily snapshot of each volume tagged Backup=daily, kept for 14 days and then deleted, without writing or running any scripts.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: A cron job on each instance that calls the EC2 CreateSnapshot API and prunes old snapshots
options.explanation: A cron job is a script the company would have to write, run and maintain on every instance.

options.text: Amazon EBS Multi-Attach, keeping each volume attached to a second standby instance
options.explanation: Multi-Attach shares one volume between instances; it makes no point-in-time copy to restore from.

options.text: An S3 Lifecycle rule that moves the volumes' snapshots to S3 Glacier after 14 days
options.explanation: EBS snapshots aren't objects in a bucket you own, so S3 Lifecycle rules can't create or expire them.

options.text: An Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policy on the tag with a daily schedule and 14-day retention

explanation: Data Lifecycle Manager policies select EBS volumes or instances by tag, create snapshots on a schedule and delete them once they pass the retention age or count, with no scripts to maintain. A cron job is the script the company wants to avoid, Multi-Attach shares a volume rather than copying it, and S3 Lifecycle rules can't see EBS snapshots. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/snapshot-lifecycle.html

prompt:
A support center wants to know whether each of its 50,000 monthly customer emails is positive, negative, neutral or mixed, so it can route unhappy customers to senior staff. It has no machine learning experts and wants a managed service that works on the text without training a model.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Convert each email to audio with Amazon Polly and score the tone of the audio
options.explanation: Polly turns text into speech; it doesn't judge sentiment, and converting text to audio adds a step for nothing.

options.text: Run each email through Amazon Transcribe and use the sentiment in its output
options.explanation: Transcribe works on audio, and its sentiment scores come from call analytics on speech; the emails are already text.

options.text: Send each email's text to the sentiment analysis API of Amazon Comprehend
Train a sentiment classifier in Amazon SageMaker AI on labeled past emails
options.explanation: A custom model needs labeled data and someone with ML skills to train and host it, which the center lacks.

explanation: Comprehend's sentiment analysis returns POSITIVE, NEGATIVE, NEUTRAL or MIXED for a block of text using a pretrained model, singly or in batch jobs, so no ML expertise or training is needed. Polly turns text into speech, Transcribe turns speech into text, and a SageMaker model needs labeled data and someone to build it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/latest/dg/how-sentiment.html

prompt:
A legacy licensing server runs on a single Amazon EC2 instance. Its license is bound to the instance's private IP address, and the vendor's software runs on only one server at a time. The company wants the instance to come back by itself, with the same private IP address and instance ID, if the underlying host has a hardware problem.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Put the instance in an Auto Scaling group with a minimum and maximum size of one
options.explanation: Auto Scaling replaces a failed instance with a new one that has a new instance ID and private IP address.

options.text: Configure a CloudWatch alarm on the system status check that runs the EC2 recover action
Place the instance behind a Network Load Balancer with health checks on the license port
options.explanation: A load balancer stops sending traffic to an unhealthy target; it doesn't bring the instance back.

options.text: Configure a CloudWatch alarm on the instance status check that runs the EC2 reboot action
options.explanation: A reboot keeps the instance on the same faulty host, so a hardware problem remains.

explanation: Instance recovery moves the instance to new hardware while keeping its instance ID, private IP addresses, Elastic IP addresses and metadata; many instance types recover automatically, and a CloudWatch alarm on the system status check with the recover action makes it explicit. Auto Scaling replaces the instance with a new ID and IP, a load balancer only stops routing to it, and a reboot stays on the faulty host. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-instance-recover.html

prompt:
An AWS Lambda function writes orders to an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance. During flash sales the function scales to thousands of concurrent executions, the database runs out of connections, and many invocations fail with "Too many connections". The company also wants connections to recover faster when the DB instance fails over. Code changes should be minimal.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Raise max_connections in the DB parameter group to the highest value the instance class allows
options.explanation: Each connection uses database memory, so this only moves the limit, and it does nothing for failover recovery.

options.text: Set reserved concurrency on the function to 50 so it opens fewer database connections
options.explanation: Capping concurrency protects the database by throttling flash-sale orders, and it does nothing for failover recovery.

options.text: Add a read replica and send half of the function's database connections to it
options.explanation: A read replica accepts no writes, so it can't take any of the order inserts.

options.text: Put Amazon RDS Proxy between the function and the database and connect through the proxy endpoint

explanation: RDS Proxy keeps a pool of database connections and shares them across many Lambda executions, so thousands of invocations need far fewer database connections, and during a Multi-AZ failover it keeps client connections open and sends them to the new primary without waiting for DNS to change. A higher max_connections only moves the ceiling, reserved concurrency throttles orders, and a read replica can't accept writes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-proxy.html

prompt:
A company keeps a pilot light disaster recovery environment in us-west-2 for a workload that runs on 400 vCPUs of On-Demand Amazon EC2 instances in us-east-1. During a DR test, the Auto Scaling groups in us-west-2 launched only part of the required capacity, and their activity history showed errors about exceeding the vCPU limit.

What should a solutions architect do so the next failover can reach full capacity?

options.text: Request On-Demand vCPU quota increases in us-west-2 to match production, using Service Quotas
Raise the maximum size of the Auto Scaling groups in us-west-2 to the production values
options.explanation: The groups tried to launch and were refused by the Regional vCPU quota; a larger maximum hits the same quota.

options.text: Request the vCPU quota increase in us-east-1 so that it applies to every Region in the account
options.explanation: EC2 quotas are set per Region, so an increase in us-east-1 leaves us-west-2 at its old limit.

options.text: Purchase a Compute Savings Plan sized for the 400 vCPUs in us-west-2
options.explanation: A Savings Plan lowers the price of usage; it neither raises a quota nor reserves any capacity.

explanation: EC2 On-Demand instance limits are vCPU quotas set per Region in each account, so a standby Region that normally runs little keeps low quotas until you ask for more; raising them ahead of time through Service Quotas lets the DR environment scale to production size during failover. A larger group maximum still hits the quota, an increase in us-east-1 doesn't carry over, and a Savings Plan is a pricing commitment. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/servicequotas/latest/userguide/request-quota-increase.html

prompt:
Operators patch the Amazon EC2 instances of a production Auto Scaling group by logging in and running updates. Over time the instances have drifted apart, and a recent manual change took the site down. The company wants each change to ship as a new, tested AMI that replaces instances gradually while at least 90% of capacity stays in service, with an automatic rollback if the new instances fail health checks.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Run AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager on the instances during a weekly maintenance window
options.explanation: Patch Manager automates in-place patching, so instances still change after launch instead of being replaced from a tested image.

options.text: Point the launch template at the new AMI and start an instance refresh with 90% minimum healthy and rollback
Create an AMI from a patched running instance and make it the launch template's default version
options.explanation: Only instances launched later use the image, so existing ones are never replaced, and an image of a hand-patched instance isn't a tested build.

options.text: Terminate the instances together so the group relaunches them from the updated launch template
options.explanation: Replacing every instance at once drops capacity far below 90% and offers no rollback.

explanation: Immutable infrastructure replaces servers instead of changing them: a new launch template version references the tested AMI, and an instance refresh replaces instances in batches while keeping the minimum healthy percentage in service, rolling back to the previous configuration if the refresh fails. Patch Manager patches in place, an AMI set as default only affects future launches, and terminating every instance at once breaks the capacity floor. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/asg-instance-refresh.html

prompt:
An online booking system runs in eu-west-1 on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database. If the Region fails, the business requires an RPO under 1 minute and an RTO of 15 minutes, and the second Region must take some customer traffic as soon as failover starts while it scales up. Running full production capacity in two Regions is too expensive.

Which disaster recovery strategy meets these requirements?

options.text: Backup and restore, copying Aurora snapshots to a second Region every hour
options.explanation: Hourly snapshot copies mean up to an hour of lost bookings, far beyond a 1-minute RPO, and a restore takes hours.

options.text: Pilot light, with an Aurora global database secondary and the application tier defined at zero instances
options.explanation: The data is current, but the application tier must launch before the Region can serve anyone, so no traffic is taken at once.

options.text: Warm standby, with an Aurora global database secondary and a small running copy of the application tier
Multi-site active/active, with full production capacity serving traffic in both Regions
options.explanation: Running full capacity in both Regions meets the objectives but is the cost the business has ruled out.

explanation: Warm standby keeps a scaled-down but fully working copy in the second Region, so after the Aurora global database secondary is promoted (its replication lag is typically under a second) the copy serves traffic at once and scales to full size within the RTO. Hourly snapshots miss the RPO, pilot light has to launch the application tier before it takes any traffic, and active/active runs full capacity in both Regions, which is ruled out on cost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html

prompt:
A Network Load Balancer is enabled in two Availability Zones. Its target group has 2 instances in AZ A and 6 in AZ B, because capacity for the instance type was short in AZ A. Clients spread evenly across the load balancer's two zonal IP addresses, and the instances in AZ A are overloaded while those in AZ B are mostly idle. The company wants traffic spread evenly across all eight instances.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Turn on cross-zone load balancing for the load balancer or its target group
Switch the target group's routing algorithm to least outstanding requests
options.explanation: Least outstanding requests is an Application Load Balancer algorithm, and it would still balance only within each zone.

options.text: Raise the target group's deregistration delay so connections drain more slowly
options.explanation: Deregistration delay only governs how long a removed target keeps its in-flight connections.

options.text: Add a Route 53 weighted record that sends 75% of clients to the AZ B node's IP address
options.explanation: Weighting DNS toward one zone treats the symptom, breaks whenever instance counts change, and works around the load balancer's zonal failover.

explanation: Each Network Load Balancer node sends traffic only to targets in its own Availability Zone unless cross-zone load balancing is on, and for Network Load Balancers it is off by default, so with clients split evenly between the two nodes the 2 instances in AZ A take half the traffic. With cross-zone load balancing each node spreads traffic across the registered targets in all enabled zones. Least outstanding requests is an ALB setting, deregistration delay affects draining, and DNS weights are a brittle workaround. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/network-load-balancers.html

prompt:
A web application's service-level objective says that 99% of requests must complete in under 1 second. The application runs behind an Application Load Balancer. The team's CloudWatch alarm on the Average statistic of TargetResponseTime stayed in the OK state during an incident in which many users waited several seconds. The team wants an alarm that reflects the objective.

Which alarm should the team create?

options.text: An alarm on the Maximum statistic of TargetResponseTime with a threshold of 1 second
options.explanation: Maximum fires on one slow request in the period, so it alarms even when 99% of requests meet the objective.

options.text: An alarm on HealthyHostCount falling below the Auto Scaling group's desired capacity
options.explanation: Healthy hosts can still answer slowly; host count says nothing about how long users wait.

options.text: An alarm on the p99 statistic of TargetResponseTime with a threshold of 1 second
An alarm on the Sum of RequestCount rising above the application's usual daily peak
options.explanation: Request volume can rise without slowing responses, and responses can slow without a rise in volume.

explanation: An objective about the 99th percentile needs the p99 percentile statistic: TargetResponseTime supports percentiles, and an alarm on p99 above 1 second fires when more than 1% of requests take longer than the objective allows, which an average hides when most requests are fast. Maximum reacts to a single outlier, HealthyHostCount measures availability rather than latency, and RequestCount measures volume. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/load-balancer-cloudwatch-metrics.html

prompt:
A company runs 40 physical and VMware servers in its data center with a mix of Windows and Linux applications. It wants disaster recovery on AWS with an RPO of seconds and an RTO of minutes, without paying for full-size servers on AWS while it waits, and without changing the applications.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: AWS Backup for the VMware virtual machines, restoring them to Amazon EC2 after a disaster
options.explanation: Scheduled backups give an RPO of hours, restores take longer than minutes, and the physical servers aren't covered.

options.text: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery, replicating the servers' disks continuously to a staging area on AWS
AWS Application Migration Service, cutting the servers over to Amazon EC2 and running them there
options.explanation: Application Migration Service moves servers to run on AWS for good, so full-size instances would run and bill all the time.

options.text: AWS DataSync, copying the servers' file systems to Amazon S3 every 15 minutes
options.explanation: DataSync copies files, not bootable servers, and a 15-minute schedule misses an RPO of seconds.

explanation: Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates the source servers' disks continuously at block level into a low-cost staging area (small replication servers and EBS volumes) for an RPO of seconds, and launches full-size recovery instances in minutes when you fail over, with no application changes. AWS Backup takes periodic backups with RPOs of hours, Application Migration Service is for moving servers to run on AWS, and DataSync copies files rather than bootable servers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/drs/latest/userguide/what-is-drs.html

prompt:
A company requires each Amazon EC2 instance in its production accounts to run the CloudWatch agent with a standard configuration. Instances are launched by many teams from different AMIs, and engineers sometimes stop the agent while troubleshooting. The company wants the agent installed and configured on new instances and restored automatically whenever an instance drifts, without changing the teams' AMIs.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: An AWS Config rule that reports instances where the agent isn't running as noncompliant
options.explanation: A Config rule reports the drift but changes nothing on the instance, so someone still has to fix it.

options.text: A Systems Manager State Manager association that applies the agent configuration on a schedule
A user data script in each team's launch template that installs the agent at first boot
options.explanation: User data runs only at launch and depends on each team's template, so an agent stopped later stays stopped.

options.text: An AWS CloudFormation drift detection run every night on the teams' stacks
options.explanation: Drift detection compares resource properties with the template; it can't see software inside the instance.

explanation: A State Manager association runs an SSM document, such as the one that installs and configures the CloudWatch agent, on every matching managed instance when it first appears and again on a schedule, so new instances get the agent and drifted ones are put back to the defined state. A Config rule only reports, user data runs once at launch, and CloudFormation drift detection doesn't look inside instances. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-state.html

prompt:
An Aurora PostgreSQL cluster has a db.r6g.4xlarge writer and three Aurora Replicas: one db.r6g.4xlarge in a second Availability Zone and two db.r6g.large replicas used for light reporting. During a recent failover Aurora promoted one of the large replicas, and the application struggled until the team failed over again by hand. The company wants Aurora to promote the 4xlarge replica whenever the writer fails.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Point the application at the 4xlarge replica's instance endpoint so it becomes the writer after failover
options.explanation: Which instance an application connects to has no effect on which replica Aurora promotes.

options.text: Convert the cluster to an Aurora global database so that failover goes to a full-size secondary cluster
options.explanation: A global database adds a cluster in another Region; failover inside this Region still follows the replicas' promotion tiers.

options.text: Set the 4xlarge replica to promotion tier 0 and the two large replicas to a higher-numbered tier
Turn on Multi-AZ for the cluster so that a standby the size of the writer is kept in another zone
options.explanation: In Aurora, Multi-AZ means a replica in another zone, which the cluster already has; there is no separate standby, and promotion still follows the tiers.

explanation: When the writer fails, Aurora promotes the replica in the highest-priority tier (tier 0 is the highest), and among replicas in the same tier it picks the largest, so tier 0 for the 4xlarge replica and a higher number for the reporting replicas makes it the target. Connection endpoints don't choose the new writer, a global database is about Region failure, and Aurora's high availability comes from its replicas, not from a separate standby. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Concepts.AuroraHighAvailability.html

prompt:
A company runs PostgreSQL on Amazon RDS as a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment. It wants failovers to finish faster (typically under 35 seconds), lower write commit latency than with its current synchronous standby, and its standby capacity to serve read traffic. The team must stay on RDS for PostgreSQL rather than move to Aurora.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add two read replicas in other Availability Zones and promote one if the primary fails
options.explanation: Replicas replicate asynchronously and need a manual promotion with an endpoint change, so failover is slower and can lose writes.

options.text: Keep the Multi-AZ DB instance deployment and put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of it
options.explanation: RDS Proxy shortens reconnection after failover, but the standby still serves no reads and write latency is unchanged.

options.text: Move the Multi-AZ DB instance deployment to a larger class with Provisioned IOPS storage
options.explanation: More capacity changes neither the failover mechanism nor the standby's inability to serve reads.

options.text: Convert to a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment with two readable standby instances

explanation: A Multi-AZ DB cluster has a writer and two readable standbys in three Availability Zones, commits once one standby acknowledges the change, and typically fails over in under 35 seconds; the standbys serve reads through the reader endpoint. Read replicas need manual promotion and replicate asynchronously, RDS Proxy speeds up reconnection but leaves the standby unreadable, and a larger instance changes neither failover nor the standby's role. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/multi-az-db-clusters-concepts.html

prompt:
A financial firm must keep a copy of each new object from an Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1 in a bucket in us-west-2. Regulators require that 99.99% of new objects be copied within 15 minutes, and the firm wants to be alerted about any object that takes longer. Both buckets are in the same account.

Which TWO actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination bucket in us-west-2
options.explanation: Transfer Acceleration speeds client uploads over long distances; it has no effect on replication.

options.text: Turn on S3 Versioning on both the source and the destination bucket
Schedule an S3 Batch Replication job every 15 minutes from the source bucket
options.explanation: Batch Replication copies existing objects on demand; it carries no time guarantee and raises no alert for a late object.

options.text: Configure S3 Event Notifications on the destination bucket for s3:ObjectCreated events
options.explanation: Arrival events say when an object lands, not when one is late; the replication rule's own metrics and events report that.

options.text: Create a Cross-Region Replication rule with S3 Replication Time Control turned on

explanation: Replication needs Versioning on both buckets, and S3 Replication Time Control is designed to replicate 99.99% of new objects within 15 minutes, backed by an SLA; it turns on replication metrics and emits an event for any object that misses the threshold, which can drive an alert. Transfer Acceleration affects client uploads, Batch Replication is for existing objects with no time target, and creation events can't show that an object is late. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/replication-time-control.html

prompt:
A company runs an active/passive application in us-east-1 and us-west-2 behind Amazon Route 53. During a past regional event, its failover runbook depended on API calls that were slow to take effect and on tooling that ran in the impaired Region. The company wants a failover switch that stays dependable during a regional impairment, works through the Route 53 data plane rather than record changes, and lets operators move traffic deliberately instead of waiting for health checks to fail.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Route 53 failover records with health checks on each Region's load balancer
options.explanation: Failover records move traffic only when health checks fail; an operator who wants to move traffic first has to edit records.

options.text: A runbook that changes the records' values with the ChangeResourceRecordSets API
options.explanation: Editing records is a Route 53 control-plane operation, the very dependency the company wants out of its failover path.

options.text: Application Recovery Controller routing controls that drive health checks on the failover records
AWS Global Accelerator traffic dials adjusted by an AWS Lambda function in us-east-1
options.explanation: Traffic dial changes are control-plane API calls, and the function making them runs in the Region that may be impaired.

explanation: Routing controls in Application Recovery Controller (ARC) are on/off switches that Route 53 reads through health checks, so flipping one changes DNS answers through the highly available data plane, and the cluster's endpoints in five Regions accept the change even when one Region is impaired. Plain failover records move traffic only when health checks fail, editing records is a control-plane operation, and a function in us-east-1 calling the Global Accelerator API depends on the impaired Region and a control plane. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/r53recovery/latest/dg/routing-control.html

prompt:
An AWS Lambda function processes messages from an Amazon SQS queue and writes to a database that handles at most 20 concurrent connections. To protect the database, the team set the function's reserved concurrency to 20. Since then, during bursts many messages land in the dead-letter queue (maxReceiveCount is 3) even though the function never threw an error on them. The team wants the database protected without dead-lettering throttled messages.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Raise the queue's maxReceiveCount to 100 and keep reserved concurrency at 20
options.explanation: A higher count only postpones dead-lettering; the poller still hands over more batches than 20 executions can take, and each throttle uses a receive.

options.text: Lower the event source mapping's batch size to 1 so that each invocation finishes faster
options.explanation: Smaller batches mean more invocations for the same messages, so the function is throttled even more often.

options.text: Set the event source mapping's maximum concurrency to 20 instead of relying on reserved concurrency
Configure provisioned concurrency of 20 on the function in place of reserved concurrency
options.explanation: Provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialized but caps nothing, so the function could open more than 20 connections.

explanation: With reserved concurrency alone, the SQS pollers keep scaling and hand the function more batches than 20 executions can take; throttled batches return to the queue and count as receives, so they reach the dead-letter queue without ever failing. Maximum concurrency on the event source mapping limits how many concurrent invocations the pollers make, so extra messages wait in the queue instead; reserved concurrency, if kept, should be at least that value. A higher maxReceiveCount postpones the problem, smaller batches add invocations, and provisioned concurrency is no cap. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-sqs-scaling.html

prompt:
A company is deploying a 30-node Apache Cassandra cluster on Amazon EC2 in one Availability Zone for low latency. Cassandra's rack-aware replication must know which nodes share underlying hardware so that replicas of the same data are kept on separate racks. The company wants large groups of nodes isolated from each other's hardware failures, and each node must be able to learn its group from instance metadata.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: A spread placement group that places each of the 30 instances on distinct hardware
options.explanation: A spread placement group holds at most seven running instances per Availability Zone, and it exposes no group a node could use as its rack.

options.text: A partition placement group with three partitions, each mapped to a Cassandra rack
A cluster placement group that packs the 30 instances close together for low latency
options.explanation: Packing nodes close together raises the chance that one hardware failure takes out many replicas at once.

options.text: No placement group, relying on Amazon EC2 to spread the instances across hosts
options.explanation: EC2 makes no promise about how instances share hardware and gives the nodes nothing to read as their rack.

explanation: A partition placement group divides instances into logical partitions whose racks share no hardware with other partitions, and each instance can read its partition number from instance metadata, so a topology-aware database such as Cassandra can map partitions to racks and keep replicas apart. Spread groups cap at seven running instances per zone, cluster groups concentrate failure risk, and without a placement group nothing is known about shared hardware. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/placement-strategies.html

prompt:
A company serves a static website and downloadable files through Amazon CloudFront from an S3 bucket in us-east-1, and the content is already copied to a bucket in us-west-2 with Cross-Region Replication. When the us-east-1 bucket returned errors during a recent incident, the site was down until an engineer changed the distribution's origin. The company wants CloudFront to retry failed GET requests against the second bucket automatically, keeping the existing distribution and domain name.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: A second CloudFront distribution for the us-west-2 bucket, behind Route 53 failover records
options.explanation: DNS failover reacts to health checks after a delay and moves whole clients; it doesn't retry a failed request against the other bucket.

options.text: Origin Shield turned on in us-east-1 so cached copies keep serving while the bucket fails
options.explanation: Origin Shield adds a caching layer, but objects that aren't cached or have expired still go to the failing bucket.

options.text: A Lambda@Edge origin-request function that picks a bucket for each request by viewer location
options.explanation: Choosing a bucket before the request doesn't help when that bucket errors; nothing retries the request elsewhere.

options.text: An origin group with the two buckets as primary and secondary, failing over on 5xx status codes

explanation: An origin group gives a cache behavior a primary and a secondary origin; when the primary returns one of the configured status codes (such as 500, 502, 503 or 504) or can't be reached, CloudFront retries that GET, HEAD or OPTIONS request against the secondary, so failover is automatic and per request within the existing distribution. DNS failover is slower and coarser, Origin Shield only helps for cached objects, and choosing an origin up front doesn't retry on errors. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/high_availability_origin_failover.html

prompt:
A news site uses an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. Monitoring shows that 90% of the database load is SELECT queries from the article pages, and the instance's CPU is saturated during traffic peaks. The application can send read queries to a separate endpoint.

Which solution improves read performance with the LEAST change to the application?

options.text: Convert the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment and send the read queries to the standby
options.explanation: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment the standby does not serve traffic; it exists only for failover.

options.text: Create one or more read replicas and send the article pages' read queries to the replicas' endpoints
Change the storage to Provisioned IOPS SSD and raise the IOPS so that queries finish more quickly
options.explanation: The bottleneck is CPU from the volume of reads, and faster storage does not take any of that work off the instance.

options.text: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the instance so it pools the application's database connections
options.explanation: Connection pooling helps with many short connections; every query still runs on the same saturated instance.

explanation: Read replicas receive asynchronous copies of the primary's data and serve read-only queries on their own endpoints, taking the SELECT load off the primary. The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance does not accept reads, faster storage does not relieve CPU, and RDS Proxy pools connections without adding capacity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html

prompt:
An online store's product pages run the same few catalog queries against an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster thousands of times per second. The data changes only a few times a day. The company wants sub-millisecond responses for these lookups and less load on the database.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add Aurora Replicas to the cluster and send the catalog queries to the reader endpoint
options.explanation: Replicas spread the load, but each lookup is still a database query with millisecond latency, not sub-millisecond.

options.text: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the cluster and point the product pages at the proxy endpoint
options.explanation: RDS Proxy pools connections; it does not cache results, so every lookup still runs on the database.

options.text: Cache the query results in Amazon ElastiCache and have the application read from the cache first
Put DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the cluster to cache the catalog query results
options.explanation: DAX is a cache for DynamoDB tables only; it cannot sit in front of an Aurora cluster.

explanation: ElastiCache is an in-memory store with sub-millisecond reads, and caching results that rarely change (cache-aside with a TTL) removes most of the repeated queries from Aurora. Replicas still run every query, RDS Proxy only pools connections, and DAX works only with DynamoDB. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/WhatIs.html

prompt:
A self-managed database on an Amazon EC2 instance needs a single block storage volume that delivers 150,000 IOPS with consistent sub-millisecond latency.

Which Amazon EBS volume type meets these requirements?

options.text: General Purpose SSD (gp3), with the IOPS provisioned to the maximum
options.explanation: A gp3 volume can be provisioned up to 80,000 IOPS, short of the 150,000 the database needs.

options.text: Throughput Optimized HDD (st1), striped across several volumes in the OS
options.explanation: st1 is built for large sequential throughput, and the requirement is one volume with very high random IOPS.

options.text: Cold HDD (sc1), sized large enough to raise its baseline performance
options.explanation: sc1 is the lowest-cost HDD for infrequently accessed data and delivers a few hundred IOPS at most.

options.text: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Block Express, with 150,000 IOPS provisioned

explanation: io2 Block Express volumes can be provisioned up to 256,000 IOPS each with sub-millisecond latency, which is the volume type for I/O-intensive databases. gp3 tops out at 80,000 IOPS per volume, and the HDD types are built for throughput or cold data rather than random IOPS. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/provisioned-iops.html

prompt:
A company serves images and videos from an Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1. Users in Asia and Europe report slow page loads. The company wants lower latency for these users without managing copies of the content in other Regions.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket and use its accelerate endpoint in the pages
options.explanation: Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance transfers to and from the bucket, but caches nothing near the users.

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the bucket as its origin and serve the content through it
Set up S3 Cross-Region Replication to buckets in Asia and Europe and use Route 53 latency routing
options.explanation: Replication creates and maintains copies in other Regions, which the company wants to avoid.

options.text: Create an AWS Global Accelerator accelerator in front of the bucket so users reach the nearest edge
options.explanation: Global Accelerator speeds up the path to Regional endpoints but does not cache content at the edge.

explanation: CloudFront caches the objects at edge locations close to viewers, so repeat requests are served locally instead of crossing the world to us-east-1, with no copies to manage. Transfer Acceleration and Global Accelerator improve the network path but do not cache, and replication means maintaining copies. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/Introduction.html

prompt:
Field teams on several continents upload 5 GB video files over the internet to a single Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1. Uploads are slow and often fail partway, forcing a full restart.

Which TWO actions together improve upload speed and reliability? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration and have the clients upload through the accelerate endpoint
Move the bucket to the S3 Express One Zone storage class in a us-east-1 Availability Zone
options.explanation: Express One Zone gives low latency to compute in the same zone; it does nothing for distant uploads over the internet.

options.text: Spread the uploaded objects across many key prefixes to raise the bucket's request rate
options.explanation: Prefixes raise how many requests per second S3 accepts, but these uploads are limited by long-distance bandwidth, not request rate.

options.text: Have the clients use multipart upload so parts upload in parallel and failed parts are retried alone
Request a higher PUT request quota for the bucket through the Service Quotas console
options.explanation: S3 has no per-bucket PUT quota to raise; throughput scales automatically with request patterns.

explanation: Transfer Acceleration routes uploads to the nearest CloudFront edge location and across the AWS backbone to the bucket, which speeds up long-distance transfers. Multipart upload splits a large file into parts that upload in parallel, and a failed part is retried without restarting the whole file. Express One Zone, prefixes and quotas do not address distance or restarts. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/transfer-acceleration.html

prompt:
An API is served by an AWS Lambda function that loads a large machine learning model during initialization, which takes about 8 seconds. Every weekday at 09:00 traffic jumps from almost nothing to 200 concurrent requests, and the first users wait for new execution environments to initialize. The company needs consistently low latency from the first request.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Set reserved concurrency of 200 on the function so that 200 execution environments are always kept available
options.explanation: Reserved concurrency guarantees and caps how many environments may run; it does not initialize any in advance.

options.text: Raise the function's memory setting to the maximum so that initialization gets more CPU and finishes sooner
options.explanation: More memory brings more CPU and a faster init, but each new environment still has to load the model on the first request.

options.text: Raise the function's timeout to 15 minutes so that requests are not cut off while the environments initialize
options.explanation: A longer timeout only avoids errors; users still wait for initialization.

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency of 200 on a function alias, scheduled with Application Auto Scaling before 09:00

explanation: Provisioned concurrency initializes the requested number of execution environments ahead of time, so requests are served without a cold start, and Application Auto Scaling can schedule it to be in place before the 09:00 jump. Reserved concurrency only sets a limit, more memory shortens but does not remove initialization, and a longer timeout changes nothing users feel. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html

prompt:
A research team runs a tightly coupled computational fluid dynamics job across 16 Amazon EC2 instances. The nodes exchange data constantly, and the job's run time is dominated by network latency between instances.

Which placement strategy should the team use?

options.text: A spread placement group, so that each instance runs on distinct hardware
options.explanation: Spread groups place instances on separate racks to limit correlated failures, which lengthens the network path and allows only 7 instances per zone.

options.text: A partition placement group, so that each instance sits in its own partition
options.explanation: Partitions isolate groups of instances on separate racks for large distributed stores such as HDFS, not for low node-to-node latency.

options.text: A cluster placement group in a single Availability Zone
An Auto Scaling group spread across three Availability Zones
options.explanation: Spreading across zones adds inter-zone latency, the opposite of what a tightly coupled job needs.

explanation: A cluster placement group packs instances close together inside one Availability Zone for the lowest latency and highest per-flow throughput between them, which is what tightly coupled HPC needs. Spread and partition groups deliberately separate hardware for resilience, and multiple zones add latency. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/placement-strategies.html

prompt:
A mobile game sends player clickstream events at up to 50,000 records per second. A real-time leaderboard, a fraud detector and an archiving job must each read every event independently, and the fraud team must be able to re-read the last 24 hours of events after deploying a new model.

Which AWS service should ingest the events?

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon SQS standard queues
options.explanation: An SQS message is deleted once a consumer processes it, so three readers cannot each see every event or replay it later.

options.text: Amazon Data Firehose
options.explanation: Firehose buffers and delivers records to destinations; applications cannot read the stream themselves or re-read past records.

options.text: Amazon SNS standard topics
options.explanation: SNS pushes each message to subscribers once and keeps nothing, so there is no way to re-read the last 24 hours.

explanation: Kinesis Data Streams keeps records for a retention period (24 hours by default, extendable), and each consuming application reads the stream with its own position, so all three can read every event and the fraud detector can reprocess from an earlier point. SQS deletes consumed messages, Firehose only delivers to destinations, and SNS keeps nothing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/introduction.html

prompt:
A company streams JSON telemetry records from thousands of devices and wants them stored in Amazon S3 in Apache Parquet format, partitioned for Amazon Athena queries, within a few minutes of arrival. The team does not want to write or run any transformation code or servers.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Send the records to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and have an AWS Lambda consumer convert them to Parquet and write to S3
options.explanation: This works but is exactly the transformation code the team does not want to write and maintain.

options.text: Land the raw JSON in S3 and run an AWS Glue ETL job every hour that converts the new files to Parquet
options.explanation: An hourly batch job misses the few-minutes target and adds an ETL script to own.

options.text: Send the records to Amazon MSK and deploy an S3 sink connector on Amazon MSK Connect that writes Parquet
options.explanation: This means running a Kafka cluster and a connector, more infrastructure than a managed delivery stream.

options.text: Send the records to an Amazon Data Firehose stream with record format conversion to Parquet using an AWS Glue table schema

explanation: Firehose can convert incoming JSON to Parquet or ORC with a schema from the AWS Glue Data Catalog, then buffer and write it to S3 with time-based prefixes, all managed and with no code. A Lambda consumer and a Glue job both mean owning transformation code, and MSK adds a cluster to run. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/firehose/latest/dev/record-format-conversion.html

prompt:
A gaming company stores player profiles in Amazon DynamoDB. A few popular profiles are read millions of times a minute, and the company needs read latency in microseconds. The developers want to change as little application code as possible.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Put an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster in front of the table and add cache logic to the application
options.explanation: ElastiCache can serve microsecond reads, but the developers would have to write the cache-aside and invalidation code.

options.text: Add a global secondary index on the player ID so that the popular profiles are read from the index
options.explanation: An index gives another access path with the same millisecond latency; it is not a cache.

options.text: Put a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table and point the DynamoDB client at it
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode so it scales instantly with the read traffic
options.explanation: On-demand mode removes throughput planning, but every read is still a normal DynamoDB read in milliseconds.

explanation: DAX is an in-memory cache built for DynamoDB that is API-compatible with it, so the application swaps in the DAX client and gets microsecond reads for hot items without writing cache logic. ElastiCache needs that logic written, an index is not a cache, and on-demand mode does not change latency. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DAX.html

prompt:
A company has 60 VPCs in one Region and a Site-to-Site VPN to its data center. Every VPC must be able to reach every other VPC and the data center, and the network team wants to add new VPCs without touching the existing connections.

Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create VPC peering connections between every pair of VPCs and a VPN connection from each VPC to the data center
options.explanation: A full mesh needs 1,770 peering connections plus 60 VPNs, and every new VPC means changing all the others.

options.text: Attach all the VPCs and the VPN to an AWS Transit Gateway and route between them through its route tables
Expose each VPC's services through AWS PrivateLink endpoint services and create interface endpoints in every other VPC
options.explanation: PrivateLink exposes individual services in one direction; it does not give full network connectivity or reach the data center.

options.text: Peer every VPC with one central hub VPC that holds the VPN connection, and route all traffic through that hub VPC
options.explanation: VPC peering is not transitive, so traffic cannot pass through the hub VPC to other VPCs or to the VPN.

explanation: A transit gateway is a regional hub that VPCs and VPN connections attach to, and it routes transitively between all attachments, so a new VPC needs one attachment and a route. A full peering mesh grows with the square of the VPC count, peering through a hub VPC is not transitive, and PrivateLink is service-level, one-way access. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/what-is-transit-gateway.html

prompt:
An Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster has four Aurora Replicas. The application sends its reads to the reader endpoint. A reporting team has started running heavy analytical queries through the same endpoint, and the application's read latency spikes whenever reports run. The company wants the reports isolated on two larger replicas while the application keeps using the others.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Resize two replicas to a larger instance class and point the reporting tools at the cluster's reader endpoint
options.explanation: The reader endpoint balances across every replica, so reports and application reads would still share all four.

options.text: Create two custom endpoints, one for the two larger replicas used by reporting and one for the application's replicas
Add an Aurora global database secondary cluster in another Region and point the reporting tools at its reader endpoint
options.explanation: This isolates the reports but adds a second Region, cross-Region replication lag and cost the company did not ask for.

options.text: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the cluster and point both the application and the reporting tools at its read-only endpoint
options.explanation: The proxy's read-only endpoint spreads connections across all readers, so it does not keep reports off the application's replicas.

explanation: Aurora custom endpoints load-balance across a chosen set of DB instances, so one endpoint can cover the two larger reporting replicas and another the replicas the application uses. The reader endpoint and the RDS Proxy read-only endpoint both spread across all readers, and a global database solves a cross-Region problem the company does not have. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Endpoints.Custom.html

prompt:
A genomics pipeline runs on hundreds of Linux EC2 instances. Its input data sets live in Amazon S3. The pipeline needs a shared POSIX file system with sub-millisecond latency and hundreds of GB/s of aggregate throughput, which loads files from S3 on first access and exports results back to S3.

Which storage solution meets these requirements?

options.text: An Amazon EFS file system with Elastic throughput, filled from S3 by an AWS DataSync task before each run
options.explanation: EFS is a general-purpose shared file system; it is not built for hundreds of GB/s, and copying data in before each run delays the pipeline.

options.text: An Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system, with the S3 data copied in by a scheduled job
options.explanation: FSx for Windows serves SMB to Windows clients and has no link to S3, so it fits neither the Linux nodes nor the S3 workflow.

options.text: An Amazon FSx for Lustre file system linked to the S3 bucket through a data repository association
Mountpoint for Amazon S3 installed on every instance, mounting the bucket as a local file system
options.explanation: Mountpoint gives high read throughput but not full POSIX semantics, such as modifying files in place or locking.

explanation: FSx for Lustre is a high-performance parallel file system with sub-millisecond latency and throughput that scales to hundreds of GB/s; a data repository association lazy-loads objects from S3 on first access and exports changed files back. EFS is not built for that throughput, FSx for Windows serves SMB without S3 integration, and Mountpoint is not fully POSIX. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/LustreGuide/what-is.html

prompt:
A stateless web application runs in an Auto Scaling group. Traffic rises sharply every weekday morning, but the time shifts by up to an hour from week to week, and launches that start after the rise leave users waiting. Unplanned spikes also happen during the day. The team does not want to maintain schedules.

Which TWO scaling configurations together meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A predictive scaling policy that forecasts the daily pattern and launches capacity ahead of it
Scheduled actions that raise the desired capacity before the earliest likely start of the morning rise
options.explanation: Scheduled actions are the schedules the team does not want to keep up, and a fixed time over-provisions on late mornings.

options.text: A simple scaling policy on CPU utilization with a 10-minute cooldown between scaling activities
options.explanation: Simple scaling waits out its cooldown after each activity, so it reacts slowly to a fast spike.

options.text: A target tracking policy that keeps the load balancer's request count per target at a set value
A launch template that switches to burstable T3 instances in unlimited mode so instances absorb the spikes
options.explanation: Burst credits let existing instances run hotter for a while; they do not add capacity when demand outgrows the group.

explanation: Predictive scaling learns the recurring daily pattern from history and launches capacity in advance, following the shifting rise without schedules, and target tracking reacts in real time to unplanned spikes by keeping requests per target near the target value. Scheduled actions need upkeep, simple scaling is slow, and burstable instances do not add capacity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-predictive-scaling.html

prompt:
A company must move 50 TB of files from an on-premises NFS server to Amazon S3 within one week over its existing 1 Gbps internet connection, which is mostly idle. After the initial copy, changed files must be transferred every night until cutover, with integrity checks, scheduling and monitoring handled by the service.

Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Order AWS Snowball Edge devices, copy the files onto them, and ship them back to AWS for import into S3
options.explanation: Shipping covers the first copy, but the nightly changes would still need another tool, and the device turnaround eats most of the week.

options.text: Deploy an AWS DataSync agent on premises and run a scheduled DataSync task from the NFS share to the S3 bucket
Deploy an Amazon S3 File Gateway and have the on-premises servers copy all the files onto its NFS share
options.explanation: A file gateway gives on-premises access to S3; using it as a bulk mover means scripting the copies and checks yourself.

options.text: Run the AWS CLI aws s3 sync command from an on-premises server on a cron schedule against the bucket
options.explanation: This can move the data, but the team owns the scheduling, retries, integrity checks and monitoring.

explanation: At 1 Gbps, about 10 TB can move per day, so 50 TB fits in a week online. DataSync copies NFS data to S3 at high speed, verifies integrity, runs on a schedule that transfers only changes, and reports through CloudWatch. Snowball does not handle the nightly deltas, and a file gateway or CLI scripts leave scheduling and verification to the team. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datasync/latest/userguide/what-is-datasync.html

prompt:
A media company stores millions of objects in Amazon S3 Standard. Some objects are read heavily for weeks after upload and others are never read again, and no one can predict which. The company wants to lower storage costs automatically without retrieval fees or any impact on read latency.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Move the objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access with a lifecycle rule 30 days after upload
options.explanation: Standard-IA charges a retrieval fee per GB, so objects that stay popular after 30 days can cost more than before.

options.text: Move the objects to S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access with a lifecycle rule 30 days after upload
options.explanation: One Zone-IA also charges per-GB retrieval fees and keeps data in a single Availability Zone.

options.text: Move the objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval with a lifecycle rule 30 days after upload
options.explanation: Glacier Flexible Retrieval objects must be restored before they can be read, taking minutes to hours.

options.text: Move the objects to S3 Intelligent-Tiering and let it place each object by its access pattern

explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering monitors each object's access and moves it between frequent and infrequent access tiers automatically, with no retrieval fees and the same millisecond latency, for a small per-object monitoring charge. Standard-IA and One Zone-IA charge retrievals that hurt when guesses are wrong, and Glacier Flexible Retrieval needs restores. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/intelligent-tiering-overview.html

prompt:
A company runs a steady compute workload 24 hours a day and expects to keep it for 3 years. During that time it plans to move from x86 to Graviton instance families, shift some capacity to another Region, and run part of the workload on AWS Fargate.

Which purchasing option gives the largest discount while allowing all of these changes?

options.text: EC2 Instance Savings Plans for the current instance family in the current Region
options.explanation: EC2 Instance Savings Plans are tied to one instance family in one Region, so the migration and the Region move fall outside them.

options.text: Compute Savings Plans for a committed hourly spend
Convertible Reserved Instances for the current instance type
options.explanation: Convertible RIs can be exchanged for other families, but they stay in their Region and never apply to Fargate.

options.text: Spot Instances managed by an EC2 Fleet with diversified types
options.explanation: Spot can be interrupted at any time, which suits flexible jobs, not a steady workload that must keep running.

explanation: Compute Savings Plans apply a committed hourly spend to EC2 usage of any family, size, operating system or Region, and to Fargate and Lambda, so the discount follows the workload through all three changes. EC2 Instance Savings Plans and Convertible RIs are bound to a Region and do not cover Fargate, and Spot is interruptible. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/savingsplans/latest/userguide/what-is-savings-plans.html

prompt:
A company runs nightly batch jobs that render video frames on Amazon EC2. Each job saves checkpoints to Amazon S3, so a job that is stopped can resume on another instance. The jobs can run at any time during the night and use several instance types.

Which purchasing option is the MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Spot Instances across several instance types and zones
On-Demand Instances with an On-Demand Capacity Reservation
options.explanation: A Capacity Reservation guarantees capacity at the On-Demand price, the most expensive choice for interruptible work.

options.text: Dedicated Hosts allocated for the nightly batch window
options.explanation: Dedicated Hosts are for licensing or compliance needs and cost more than shared-tenancy instances.

options.text: Standard Reserved Instances on a 1-year term
options.explanation: Reserved Instances bill for every hour of the term, so instances used only at night pay for idle daytime hours.

explanation: Spot Instances use spare EC2 capacity at a large discount from On-Demand and can be reclaimed with a two-minute warning, which checkpointed, flexible batch jobs tolerate well; spreading across types and zones reduces interruptions. Capacity Reservations and Dedicated Hosts cost more, and Reserved Instances charge around the clock. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/using-spot-instances.html

prompt:
Applications in private subnets upload several terabytes per day to Amazon S3 buckets in the same Region through a NAT gateway. The NAT gateway's data processing charges have become a large part of the bill.

Which change reduces this cost the MOST?

options.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for S3 and update the applications to use the endpoint's DNS name
options.explanation: Interface endpoints charge by the hour and per GB processed, so they cost more than a gateway endpoint for this traffic.

options.text: Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance on a small EC2 instance type in the public subnet
options.explanation: A NAT instance avoids the per-GB charge but must carry terabytes a day, needs managing, and is a single point of failure.

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and add it to the private subnets' route tables
Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the buckets so the uploads leave through the nearest edge location
options.explanation: Transfer Acceleration adds a per-GB charge and still sends the traffic out through the NAT gateway.

explanation: A gateway endpoint for S3 adds a route that sends S3 traffic straight from the VPC to S3, bypassing the NAT gateway, and gateway endpoints carry no hourly or data processing charge. Interface endpoints are billed, a NAT instance trades cost for operational risk, and Transfer Acceleration adds cost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html

prompt:
An application writes log files to Amazon S3. Logs are read often for 30 days, occasionally from day 30 to day 90, and after that only during audits, when they must be available within 12 hours. Logs must be kept for 7 years and then deleted.

Which lifecycle configuration is the MOST cost-effective?

options.text: S3 Standard, then S3 Standard-IA at 30 days, then S3 Glacier Deep Archive at 90 days, and expire after 7 years
S3 Standard, then S3 Standard-IA at 30 days, then S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval at 90 days, and expire after 7 years
options.explanation: Glacier Instant Retrieval gives millisecond access at a much higher storage price than Deep Archive, and audits allow 12 hours.

options.text: S3 Standard, then S3 One Zone-IA at 30 days, then S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 90 days, and expire after 7 years
options.explanation: Glacier Flexible Retrieval costs more to store than Deep Archive and its faster restores are not needed for audits.

options.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering from upload, with no archive tiers enabled, and expire after 7 years
options.explanation: Without archive tiers the oldest logs stay in the infrequent access tiers, far more expensive than Deep Archive.

explanation: Standard-IA suits the occasional reads from day 30 to 90, and S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost storage class, with standard retrievals completing within 12 hours, which meets the audit requirement for the remaining years before expiration. Instant Retrieval and Flexible Retrieval cost more than the audit window requires, and Intelligent-Tiering without archive tiers never gets that low. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html

prompt:
An internal tool uses a MySQL-compatible database that is busy for a few hours a day at unpredictable times and idle the rest of the time, including whole weekends. It currently runs on a provisioned Amazon Aurora MySQL instance sized for its peak. The company wants to stop paying for idle compute with minimal operational effort.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Buy a 1-year Reserved Instance for the current Aurora instance class to lower its hourly price
options.explanation: A Reserved Instance lowers the rate but still bills every hour, including all the idle ones.

options.text: Migrate to Amazon RDS for MySQL and add a Lambda function that stops the instance when it has been idle for an hour
options.explanation: Someone has to own the idle detection and the start-up path, and a stopped RDS instance restarts itself after 7 days.

options.text: Move the database to Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity so it is billed only per request
options.explanation: DynamoDB is not MySQL-compatible, so the tool would need rewriting.

options.text: Move the cluster to Aurora Serverless v2 with a minimum capacity of 0 ACUs so it pauses when idle

explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity with demand, and with a minimum of 0 ACUs it pauses automatically after a period without connections and resumes on the next one, so idle hours cost only storage. A Reserved Instance still bills idle time, a stop-start function is home-made automation, and DynamoDB is not MySQL. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-serverless-v2-auto-pause.html

prompt:
A DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode serves a mature application. Its traffic has been nearly flat at about 4,000 reads and 1,000 writes per second, around the clock, for a year, and the table holds 200 GB that is read constantly. The company wants to cut the table's cost significantly for the next 3 years.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Switch the table to provisioned capacity sized to the steady load and buy DynamoDB reserved capacity for it
Keep on-demand mode and switch the table to the DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access table class
options.explanation: Standard-IA lowers storage price but raises the per-request price, which is the wrong trade for a table read constantly.

options.text: Keep on-demand mode and put a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table for the reads
options.explanation: DAX adds node costs, and it only saves money when most reads hit the same cached items.

options.text: Switch the table to provisioned capacity with auto scaling that has a wide range and no reserved capacity
options.explanation: Provisioned capacity already beats on-demand for flat traffic, but without a reservation the 3-year commitment brings no discount.

explanation: For flat, predictable traffic, provisioned capacity costs less than paying per request, and reserved capacity adds a further discount for committing to a level of throughput for one or three years. The Standard-IA table class suits tables dominated by storage rather than throughput, DAX adds cost unless reads are highly repetitive, and provisioned capacity without a reservation leaves the long-term discount unused. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/capacity-mode.html

prompt:
A small company runs a thumbnail service on an On-Demand m5.large instance that runs all the time. Users upload about 200 images a day to an Amazon S3 bucket, and each thumbnail takes about 3 seconds to generate. The instance is idle more than 99% of the time.

Which solution is the MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Move the service to a t3.micro On-Demand instance that runs all the time and polls the bucket for new images
options.explanation: A smaller instance is cheaper, but it still bills every hour of the day for a few minutes of daily work.

options.text: Run the service as an AWS Lambda function invoked by S3 event notifications when images are uploaded
Move the service to a Spot Instance that runs all the time and is replaced automatically when interrupted
options.explanation: Spot lowers the hourly price, but it still bills for an always-on instance that is almost always idle.

options.text: Run the service as an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate with one task that runs all the time
options.explanation: An always-running Fargate task bills for its vCPU and memory every second, idle or not.

explanation: Lambda bills only for invocations and compute time, so 200 three-second runs a day cost a tiny amount, and S3 event notifications invoke the function directly with nothing to poll. Every option that keeps a server or task running pays for idle time, however small or discounted it is. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/with-s3.html

prompt:
A software company distributes installers from an Amazon S3 bucket to the public through direct S3 URLs. Anonymous users around the world download the same few files many times, and data transfer out from S3 is now the largest item on the bill.

Which solution reduces data transfer costs the MOST?

options.text: Turn on Requester Pays for the bucket so the people downloading the installers pay for the transfer
options.explanation: Requester Pays works only for authenticated AWS requesters, so anonymous public downloads would be refused.

options.text: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket and publish the accelerated download URLs instead
options.explanation: Transfer Acceleration charges more per GB, on top of the normal transfer price.

options.text: Serve the files through an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the bucket as its origin
Move the bucket to the AWS Region with the lowest S3 storage price and update the download links
options.explanation: Storage price is not the problem; every download still pays S3 data transfer out from whichever Region it is in.

explanation: CloudFront serves repeat downloads from its edge caches, so most requests never reach the bucket, and on the CloudFront pricing page transfer from AWS origins such as S3 to CloudFront is free, with transfer out to viewers generally priced below S3's. Requester Pays refuses anonymous access, Transfer Acceleration adds charges, and moving Regions does not change transfer out. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/ConfiguringCaching.html

prompt:
A development environment runs 40 On-Demand EC2 instances with gp2 EBS volumes. Developers use it only from 08:00 to 18:00 on weekdays, and the instances are stateless apart from their EBS volumes. The company wants to cut the environment's cost without affecting developers during working hours.

Which TWO actions together meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Stop the instances outside working hours on a schedule, for example with the Instance Scheduler on AWS solution
Buy 3-year All Upfront Reserved Instances for the 40 development instances
options.explanation: Reserved Instances bill for every hour of the term, and these instances are needed for only about 30% of the week.

options.text: Migrate the gp2 volumes to gp3, which costs less per GB at the same baseline performance
Move the instances to Dedicated Instances so that they run on hardware reserved for the company
options.explanation: Dedicated Instances carry a higher price than shared tenancy and do nothing to reduce idle hours.

options.text: Migrate the gp2 volumes to io2 so that the instances start faster each morning after being stopped
options.explanation: io2 volumes cost more per GB and bill for provisioned IOPS, raising cost rather than lowering it.

explanation: Stopped instances do not bill for compute, so stopping them for nights and weekends removes about 70% of instance hours, and gp3 is priced lower per GB than gp2 while giving a 3,000 IOPS baseline that can be changed in place. Reserved Instances bill around the clock, Dedicated Instances cost more, and io2 is a premium volume type. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/solutions/latest/instance-scheduler-on-aws/solution-overview.html

prompt:
A company stores 20 TB of project files on an Amazon EFS Regional file system used by Linux application servers. Most files are not opened again after 30 days, but when one is, the application must read it through the same mount path. The data must stay replicated across Availability Zones.

Which solution reduces storage cost with the LEAST change to the application?

options.text: Recreate the file system as an EFS One Zone file system and copy the files across with AWS DataSync
options.explanation: One Zone storage is cheaper, but it keeps data in a single Availability Zone, which breaks the replication requirement.

options.text: Set an EFS lifecycle policy that moves files to Infrequent Access after 30 days without access
Move files older than 30 days to an S3 bucket with a nightly script and change the application to read them from S3
options.explanation: S3 storage is cheaper, but the application would need changes to read old files from a different place.

options.text: Switch the file system from Elastic throughput to Provisioned throughput set to the average load
options.explanation: Throughput mode changes what you pay for throughput, not the per-GB price of storing 20 TB.

explanation: EFS lifecycle management moves files that have not been accessed for a set period into the lower-cost Infrequent Access storage class, still Regional and multi-AZ, and the files stay at the same paths. One Zone gives up multi-AZ replication, moving files to S3 changes the application, and throughput settings do not change storage price. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/lifecycle-management-efs.html

prompt:
A stateless web application runs in an Auto Scaling group. It needs at least 10 instances at all times, and unpredictable peaks push it to 40 instances for a few hours several times a week. The application tolerates individual instances being replaced. The company wants the lowest cost without risking the 10-instance baseline.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use only Spot Instances across several instance types, with a minimum group size of 10
options.explanation: If Spot capacity is reclaimed, nothing guarantees the 10-instance baseline the application needs.

options.text: Buy Reserved Instances for 40 instances so that every peak is covered at the discounted rate
options.explanation: Reserving for the peak pays for 30 instances that sit idle most of the week.

options.text: Use a mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base of 10 covered by a Savings Plan and Spot above the base
Use On-Demand Instances only, with scheduled actions that raise capacity to 40 on the busiest weekdays
options.explanation: The peaks are unpredictable, so schedules miss some and over-provision others, all at the On-Demand price.

explanation: A mixed instances policy can keep a base capacity of On-Demand Instances, here 10 discounted by a Savings Plan commitment, and fill everything above it with Spot Instances across several types, so the baseline is safe and peaks are cheap. All-Spot risks the baseline, reserving for the peak wastes most of it, and schedules do not fit unpredictable peaks. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-mixed-instances-groups.html

prompt:
An Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster runs an I/O-heavy order processing workload. Cost reports show that storage I/O requests are about 40% of the cluster's monthly Aurora charges, and the I/O volume is expected to grow. The company wants to lower and stabilize the cluster's cost without changing the application.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Switch the cluster's storage configuration from Aurora Standard to Aurora I/O-Optimized
Convert the cluster's instances to Aurora Serverless v2 so that capacity follows the workload
options.explanation: Serverless v2 changes how compute is billed; under Aurora Standard the I/O requests are still charged.

options.text: Add Aurora Replicas and move the order queries to the reader endpoint to spread the I/O across instances
options.explanation: Replicas share the same cluster volume, so the I/O is still billed, and the replicas add instance cost.

options.text: Change the cluster volume to Provisioned IOPS storage so that I/O is billed at a fixed provisioned rate
options.explanation: Aurora storage is not provisioned that way; Provisioned IOPS volumes belong to RDS instances, not Aurora clusters.

explanation: Aurora I/O-Optimized charges nothing for read and write I/O in exchange for higher instance and storage prices, and AWS recommends it when I/O exceeds about 25% of Aurora spend, which makes cost both lower and predictable as I/O grows. Serverless v2 and replicas leave I/O billed, and Aurora has no Provisioned IOPS volume to choose. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/Aurora.Overview.StorageReliability.html

prompt:
Amazon ECS tasks on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets pull large container images from Amazon ECR and write heavily to Amazon DynamoDB, all in the same Region. All of this traffic goes through a NAT gateway, and its data processing charges are high. The company wants the largest saving for the least ongoing cost.

Which TWO actions together meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for DynamoDB and add it to the private subnets' route tables
Create an interface VPC endpoint for DynamoDB in each private subnet's Availability Zone
options.explanation: DynamoDB interface endpoints bill by the hour and per GB, where a gateway endpoint carries the same traffic at no charge.

options.text: Add a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone so that tasks stop sending traffic across zones
